Noble patricians, patrons of my right, / Defend the justice of my cause with arms; / And, countrymen, my loving followers, / Plead my successive title with your swords. / I am his firstborn son that was the last / That wore the imperial diadem of Rome; / Then let my father's honours live in me, / Nor wrong mine age with this indignity.

Noble lords, protectors of my rights, defend the justice of my claim with weapons. And you, my countrymen and loyal followers, argue my right of succession with your swords. I am the eldest son of the last man who wore the imperial crown of Rome. So let my father's honours live on in me, and do not insult my seniority with this outrage.

Romans, friends, followers, favourers of my right, / If ever Bassianus, Caesar's son, / Were gracious in the eyes of royal Rome, / Keep then this passage to the Capitol, / And suffer not dishonour to approach / The imperial seat, to virtue consecrate, / To justice, continence, and nobility; / But let desert in pure election shine, / And, Romans, fight for freedom in your choice.

Romans, friends, followers and supporters of my cause: if Bassianus, Caesar's son, was ever well thought of by royal Rome, then guard this way to the Capitol. Do not let dishonour come near the emperor's throne, which is dedicated to virtue, justice, self-control and nobility. Let merit shine out in a free election, and, Romans, fight for the freedom to choose.

Princes, that strive by factions and by friends / Ambitiously for rule and empery, / Know that the people of Rome, for whom we stand / A special party, have by common voice, / In election for the Roman empery, / Chosen Andronicus, surnamed Pius / For many good and great deserts to Rome. / A nobler man, a braver warrior, / Lives not this day within the city walls. / He by the senate is accited home / From weary wars against the barbarous Goths, / That with his sons, a terror to our foes, / Hath yoked a nation strong, trained up in arms. / Ten years are spent since first he undertook / This cause of Rome, and chastised with arms / Our enemies' pride. Five times he hath returned / Bleeding to Rome, bearing his valiant sons / In coffins from the field. / And now at last, laden with honour's spoils, / Returns the good Andronicus to Rome, / Renowned Titus, flourishing in arms. / Let us entreat, by honour of his name / Whom worthily you would have now succeed, / And in the Capitol and senate's right, / Whom you pretend to honour and adore, / That you withdraw you and abate your strength, / Dismiss your followers, and, as suitors should, / Plead your deserts in peace and humbleness.

Princes, you who are competing for power through parties and supporters: know that the people of Rome, whom we tribunes represent, have chosen by a common vote, in this election for emperor, Andronicus, surnamed Pius (the dutiful), for his many great services to Rome. There is no nobler man or braver warrior alive within the city walls today. The senate has called him home from tiring wars against the barbarous Goths, a strong and warlike nation that he and his sons, a terror to our enemies, have conquered. Ten years have passed since he took up Rome's cause and began punishing our enemies' pride. Five times he has come back to Rome bleeding, carrying his brave sons home from the battlefield in coffins. And now at last good Andronicus, famous Titus, returns to Rome loaded with the spoils of honour, at the height of his success in war. In the name of the man you would have succeed your father, and out of respect for the Capitol and the senate, which you claim to honour, we ask you to withdraw, reduce your forces, dismiss your followers, and argue your claims peacefully and humbly, as candidates should.
How fair the tribune speaks to calm my thoughts!
How kindly the tribune speaks to calm me down!

Marcus Andronicus, so I do affy / In thy uprightness and integrity, / And so I love and honour thee and thine, / Thy noble brother Titus and his sons, / And her to whom my thoughts are humbled all, / Gracious Lavinia, Rome's rich ornament, / That I will here dismiss my loving friends, / And to my fortunes and the people's favour / Commit my cause in balance to be weighed.

Marcus Andronicus, I trust so much in your honesty and integrity, and I love and honour you and your family so much, your noble brother Titus and his sons, and the one to whom all my thoughts bow down, gracious Lavinia, Rome's richest jewel, that I will dismiss my loyal friends here and leave my cause to fortune and to the people's favour, to be weighed in the balance.
Friends, that have been thus forward in my right, / I thank you all and here dismiss you all, / And to the love and favour of my country / Commit myself, my person, and the cause.
Friends, who have been so eager to support my claim, I thank you all and dismiss you all, and I trust myself, my person and my cause to the love and goodwill of my country.
Rome, be as just and gracious unto me / As I am confident and kind to thee. / Open the gates and let me in.
Rome, be as fair and kind to me as I am trusting and kind to you. Open the gates and let me in.
Tribunes, and me, a poor competitor.
Let me in too, tribunes, a humble rival.

Romans, make way! The good Andronicus, / Patron of virtue, Rome's best champion, / Successful in the battles that he fights, / With honour and with fortune is returned / From where he circumscribed with his sword / And brought to yoke the enemies of Rome.

Romans, make way! The good Andronicus, champion of virtue and Rome's greatest defender, victorious in every battle he fights, has returned with honour and good fortune from the lands where his sword has cut down the enemies of Rome and forced them under the yoke.

Hail, Rome, victorious in thy mourning weeds! / Lo, as the bark that hath discharged her fraught / Returns with precious lading to the bay / From whence at first she weighed her anchorage, / Cometh Andronicus, bound with laurel boughs, / To resalute his country with his tears, / Tears of true joy for his return to Rome. / Thou great defender of this Capitol, / Stand gracious to the rites that we intend. / Romans, of five-and-twenty valiant sons, / Half of the number that King Priam had, / Behold the poor remains, alive and dead. / These that survive let Rome reward with love; / These that I bring unto their latest home, / With burial amongst their ancestors. / Here Goths have given me leave to sheathe my sword. / Titus, unkind, and careless of thine own, / Why suffer'st thou thy sons, unburied yet, / To hover on the dreadful shore of Styx? / Make way to lay them by their brethren.

Hail, Rome, victorious even in your mourning clothes! Like a ship that has unloaded her cargo and returns with a precious load to the harbour where she first raised her anchor, Andronicus comes home, crowned with laurel, to greet his country again with tears, tears of real joy at his return to Rome. Jupiter, great protector of this Capitol, look kindly on the rites we are about to perform. Romans, of my twenty-five brave sons, half as many as King Priam had, look at what is left, the living and the dead. Let Rome reward those who survive with love. These, whom I bring to their final home, let Rome reward with burial among their ancestors. Here the Goths have let me put away my sword. Titus, you unkind father, careless of your own, why do you leave your sons unburied, hovering on the dreadful bank of the river Styx? Make way to lay them beside their brothers.

There greet in silence, as the dead are wont, / And sleep in peace, slain in your country's wars. / O sacred receptacle of my joys, / Sweet cell of virtue and nobility, / How many sons hast thou of mine in store, / That thou wilt never render to me more?

Greet each other there in silence, as the dead do, and sleep in peace, killed in your country's wars. O sacred store of my joys, sweet cell of virtue and nobility, how many of my sons do you keep that you will never give back to me?

Give us the proudest prisoner of the Goths, / That we may hew his limbs, and on a pile / Ad manes fratrum sacrifice his flesh / Before this earthy prison of their bones, / That so the shadows be not unappeased, / Nor we disturbed with prodigies on earth.

Give us the proudest of the Gothic prisoners, so that we can hack off his limbs and sacrifice his flesh on a pyre to the spirits of our brothers, in front of this earthly prison of their bones. Then their ghosts will not go unsatisfied, and we will not be troubled by evil omens on earth.
I give him you, the noblest that survives, / The eldest son of this distressed queen.
I give you him, the noblest one alive: the eldest son of this grieving queen.

Stay, Roman brethren! Gracious conqueror, / Victorious Titus, rue the tears I shed, / A mother's tears in passion for her son. / And if thy sons were ever dear to thee, / O, think my son to be as dear to me. / Sufficeth not that we are brought to Rome, / To beautify thy triumphs and return / Captive to thee and to thy Roman yoke; / But must my sons be slaughtered in the streets / For valiant doings in their country's cause? / O, if to fight for king and commonweal / Were piety in thine, it is in these. / Andronicus, stain not thy tomb with blood. / Wilt thou draw near the nature of the gods? / Draw near them then in being merciful. / Sweet mercy is nobility's true badge. / Thrice-noble Titus, spare my first-born son.

Wait, Roman brothers! Gracious conqueror, victorious Titus, pity the tears I shed, a mother's tears of grief for her son. If your sons were ever dear to you, then think that my son is just as dear to me. Is it not enough that we are brought to Rome to decorate your triumph, captives under your Roman yoke? Must my sons be slaughtered in the streets as well, for fighting bravely for their country? If fighting for king and country was a sacred duty for your sons, it was the same for mine. Andronicus, do not stain your tomb with blood. Do you want to come close to the nature of the gods? Then come close to them by being merciful. Sweet mercy is the true badge of nobility. Thrice-noble Titus, spare my first-born son.

Patient yourself, madam, and pardon me. / These are their brethren whom your Goths beheld / Alive and dead, and for their brethren slain / Religiously they ask a sacrifice. / To this your son is marked, and die he must, / T' appease their groaning shadows that are gone.

Be patient, madam, and forgive me. These are the brothers of the men your Goths saw alive and dead, and for their brothers who were killed they ask for a sacrifice, as religion demands. Your son is marked out for it, and he must die, to satisfy the groaning ghosts of the dead.
Away with him, and make a fire straight, / And with our swords, upon a pile of wood, / Let's hew his limbs till they be clean consumed.
Take him away, and build a fire at once, and let us hack his limbs with our swords on a pile of wood until they are completely burned.
Was never Scythia half so barbarous!
Even Scythia was never half so barbaric!

Oppose not Scythia to ambitious Rome. / Alarbus goes to rest, and we survive / To tremble under Titus' threat'ning look. / Then, madam, stand resolved, but hope withal / The self-same gods that armed the Queen of Troy / With opportunity of sharp revenge / Upon the Thracian tyrant in his tent / May favour Tamora, the queen of Goths, / (When Goths were Goths and Tamora was queen) / To quit the bloody wrongs upon her foes.

Don't compare Scythia with ambitious Rome. Alarbus goes to his rest, and we live on to tremble under Titus's threatening look. So, madam, stand firm, but hope as well that the same gods who gave Hecuba, Queen of Troy, the chance of sharp revenge on the Thracian tyrant in his tent may favour Tamora, Queen of the Goths (when the Goths were still Goths and Tamora was queen), to repay her enemies for these bloody wrongs.

See, lord and father, how we have performed / Our Roman rites. Alarbus' limbs are lopped, / And entrails feed the sacrificing fire, / Whose smoke like incense doth perfume the sky. / Remaineth naught but to inter our brethren, / And with loud 'larums welcome them to Rome.

See, my lord and father, how we have carried out our Roman rites. Alarbus's limbs have been cut off, and his entrails feed the sacrificial fire, whose smoke perfumes the sky like incense. All that is left is to bury our brothers and welcome them to Rome with loud trumpet calls.
Let it be so; and let Andronicus / Make this his latest farewell to their souls.
Let it be so. And let Andronicus say his last farewell to their souls.

In peace and honour rest you here, my sons; / Rome's readiest champions, repose you here in rest, / Secure from worldly chances and mishaps. / Here lurks no treason, here no envy swells, / Here grow no damned drugs; here are no storms, / No noise, but silence and eternal sleep. / In peace and honour rest you here, my sons.

Rest here in peace and honour, my sons. Rome's readiest champions, lie here at rest, safe from the chances and accidents of the world. No treason lurks here, no envy swells, no cursed poisons grow; there are no storms here, no noise, only silence and eternal sleep. Rest here in peace and honour, my sons.

In peace and honour live Lord Titus long; / My noble lord and father, live in fame. / Lo, at this tomb my tributary tears / I render for my brethren's obsequies; / And at thy feet I kneel, with tears of joy / Shed on this earth for thy return to Rome. / O, bless me here with thy victorious hand, / Whose fortunes Rome's best citizens applaud.

May Lord Titus live long in peace and honour. My noble lord and father, live on in fame. Look, at this tomb I offer my tears as a tribute at my brothers' funeral. And I kneel at your feet with tears of joy, shed on this ground for your return to Rome. O, bless me here with your victorious hand, whose achievements Rome's best citizens applaud.
Kind Rome, that hast thus lovingly reserved / The cordial of mine age to glad my heart! / Lavinia, live; outlive thy father's days, / And fame's eternal date, for virtue's praise.
Kind Rome, which has kept safe for me the comfort of my old age to cheer my heart! Lavinia, live. Outlive your father's days and the everlasting span of fame, through praise of your virtue.
Long live Lord Titus, my beloved brother, / Gracious triumpher in the eyes of Rome.
Long live Lord Titus, my beloved brother, a gracious conqueror in the eyes of Rome.
Thanks, gentle tribune, noble brother Marcus.
Thank you, kind tribune, my noble brother Marcus.

And welcome, nephews, from successful wars, / You that survive, and you that sleep in fame. / Fair lords, your fortunes are alike in all, / That in your country's service drew your swords; / But safer triumph is this funeral pomp / That hath aspired to Solon's happiness / And triumphs over chance in honour's bed. / Titus Andronicus, the people of Rome, / Whose friend in justice thou hast ever been, / Send thee by me, their tribune and their trust, / This palliament of white and spotless hue, / And name thee in election for the empire / With these our late-deceased emperor's sons. / Be candidatus then, and put it on, / And help to set a head on headless Rome.

And welcome, nephews, home from successful wars: those of you who survive, and those who sleep in glory. Noble lords, your fortunes are equal in this, that you all drew your swords in your country's service. But this funeral procession is a safer triumph. It has reached the happiness Solon spoke of, which no one can call happy until death, and it triumphs over chance in the bed of honour. Titus Andronicus, the people of Rome, whose friend in justice you have always been, send you this white and spotless robe by me, their tribune and the one they trust. They name you as a candidate for emperor alongside these sons of our late emperor. Be a candidate, then, and put it on, and help to give headless Rome a head.

A better head her glorious body fits / Than his that shakes for age and feebleness. / What, should I don this robe and trouble you? / Be chosen with proclamations today, / Tomorrow yield up rule, resign my life, / And set abroad new business for you all? / Rome, I have been thy soldier forty years, / And led my country's strength successfully, / And buried one and twenty valiant sons, / Knighted in field, slain manfully in arms, / In right and service of their noble country. / Give me a staff of honour for mine age, / But not a sceptre to control the world. / Upright he held it, lords, that held it last.

A better head than mine suits her glorious body, a head that does not shake with age and weakness. What, should I put on this robe and trouble you? Be chosen with proclamations today, give up power and die tomorrow, and leave you all with fresh business? Rome, I have been your soldier for forty years. I have led my country's armies successfully, and I have buried twenty-one brave sons, knighted on the battlefield and killed bravely in arms, fighting for their noble country. Give me a staff of honour for my old age, but not a sceptre to rule the world. The man who held it last, lords, held it with honour.
Titus, thou shalt obtain and ask the empery.
Titus, you only have to ask, and you will have the empire.
Proud and ambitious tribune, canst thou tell?
Proud, ambitious tribune, how can you know that?

Romans, do me right. / Patricians, draw your swords, and sheathe them not / Till Saturninus be Rome's emperor. / Andronicus, would thou were shipped to hell / Rather than rob me of the people's hearts!

Romans, give me justice. Lords, draw your swords and do not put them away until Saturninus is Rome's emperor. Andronicus, I wish you were shipped to hell rather than that you should steal the people's hearts from me!
Proud Saturnine, interrupter of the good / That noble-minded Titus means to thee!
Proud Saturnine, you are getting in the way of the good that noble Titus means to do for you!
Content thee, prince; I will restore to thee / The people's hearts, and wean them from themselves.
Calm yourself, prince. I will give the people's hearts back to you, and wean them away from their own choice.

Andronicus, I do not flatter thee, / But honour thee, and will do till I die. / My faction if thou strengthen with thy friends, / I will most thankful be; and thanks to men / Of noble minds is honourable meed.

Andronicus, I do not flatter you, but I honour you and will do until I die. If you strengthen my party with your friends, I will be very grateful, and to men of noble minds thanks is an honourable reward.
People of Rome, and people's tribunes here, / I ask your voices and your suffrages. / Will you bestow them friendly on Andronicus?
People of Rome, and tribunes of the people here, I ask for your voices and your votes. Will you give them as friends to Andronicus?
To gratify the good Andronicus, / And gratulate his safe return to Rome, / The people will accept whom he admits.
To please the good Andronicus and to celebrate his safe return to Rome, the people will accept whoever he approves.

Tribunes, I thank you; and this suit I make, / That you create your emperor's eldest son, / Lord Saturnine; whose virtues will, I hope, / Reflect on Rome as Titan's rays on earth, / And ripen justice in this commonweal. / Then, if you will elect by my advice, / Crown him, and say "Long live our emperor!"

Tribunes, I thank you. And this is my request: that you make our late emperor's eldest son, Lord Saturnine, emperor. I hope his virtues will shine on Rome as the sun's rays shine on the earth, and ripen justice in this state. So, if you will elect on my advice, crown him and say 'Long live our emperor!'
With voices and applause of every sort, / Patricians and plebeians, we create / Lord Saturninus Rome's great emperor, / And say "Long live our Emperor Saturnine!"
With the voices and applause of every rank, lords and common people, we make Lord Saturninus Rome's great emperor, and say 'Long live our Emperor Saturnine!'

Titus Andronicus, for thy favours done / To us in our election this day, / I give thee thanks in part of thy deserts, / And will with deeds requite thy gentleness. / And for an onset, Titus, to advance / Thy name and honourable family, / Lavinia will I make my empress, / Rome's royal mistress, mistress of my heart, / And in the sacred Pantheon her espouse. / Tell me, Andronicus, doth this motion please thee?

Titus Andronicus, for the favours you have done me in my election today, I thank you as part of what you deserve, and I will repay your kindness with deeds. And to begin with, Titus, to raise up your name and your honourable family, I will make Lavinia my empress, Rome's royal mistress and mistress of my heart, and marry her in the sacred Pantheon. Tell me, Andronicus, does this proposal please you?

It doth, my worthy lord, and in this match / I hold me highly honoured of your grace; / And here in sight of Rome, to Saturnine, / King and commander of our commonweal, / The wide world's emperor, do I consecrate / My sword, my chariot, and my prisoners; / Presents well worthy Rome's imperious lord. / Receive them then, the tribute that I owe, / Mine honour's ensigns humbled at thy feet.

It does, my worthy lord, and I consider myself greatly honoured by your grace in this match. And here, in the sight of Rome, I dedicate to Saturnine, king and ruler of our state and emperor of the wide world, my sword, my chariot and my prisoners: gifts well worthy of Rome's commanding lord. Receive them, then, the tribute that I owe, the signs of my honour laid humbly at your feet.

Thanks, noble Titus, father of my life. / How proud I am of thee and of thy gifts / Rome shall record, and when I do forget / The least of these unspeakable deserts, / Romans, forget your fealty to me.
Thank you, noble Titus, father of my new life. Rome shall record how proud I am of you and your gifts, and when I forget the smallest of these immense services, Romans, forget your loyalty to me.
[To Tamora] Now, madam, are you prisoner to an emperor; / To him that for your honour and your state / Will use you nobly and your followers.
(To Tamora) Now, madam, you are the prisoner of an emperor, who, for the sake of your honour and your rank, will treat you and your followers nobly.

A goodly lady, trust me, of the hue / That I would choose, were I to choose anew. / Clear up, fair queen, that cloudy countenance. / Though chance of war hath wrought this change of cheer, / Thou com'st not to be made a scorn in Rome. / Princely shall be thy usage every way. / Rest on my word, and let not discontent / Daunt all your hopes. Madam, he comforts you / Can make you greater than the Queen of Goths. / Lavinia, you are not displeased with this?

A fine lady, believe me, with the very looks I would choose if I were choosing again. Brighten up, fair queen, and clear that cloudy face. Though the fortunes of war have brought about this change in your mood, you have not come to be mocked in Rome. You will be treated like a princess in every way. Trust my word, and do not let unhappiness crush all your hopes. Madam, the man who comforts you can make you greater than the Queen of the Goths. Lavinia, you are not offended by this?
Not I, my lord, sith true nobility / Warrants these words in princely courtesy.
Not I, my lord, since true nobility guarantees that these words are only royal courtesy.
Thanks, sweet Lavinia. Romans, let us go. / Ransomless here we set our prisoners free. / Proclaim our honours, lords, with trump and drum.
Thank you, sweet Lavinia. Romans, let us go. We set our prisoners free here without ransom. Lords, proclaim our honours with trumpet and drum.
Lord Titus, by your leave, this maid is mine.
Lord Titus, with your permission, this girl is mine.
How, sir? Are you in earnest then, my lord?
What, sir? Do you mean it, my lord?
Ay, noble Titus; and resolved withal / To do myself this reason and this right.
Yes, noble Titus, and I am determined to claim what is reasonable and right for me.
Suum cuique is our Roman justice. / This prince in justice seizeth but his own.
'To each his own' is our Roman justice. This prince is only taking what is rightfully his.
And that he will and shall, if Lucius live.
And he will, and shall, as long as Lucius is alive.
Traitors, avaunt! Where is the emperor's guard?
Traitors, get back! Where is the emperor's guard?
Treason, my lord, Lavinia is surprised.
Treason, my lord! Lavinia has been seized.
By him that justly may / Bear his betrothed from all the world away.
By the man who has every right to carry off his promised bride, away from all the world.
Brothers, help to convey her hence away, / And with my sword I'll keep this door safe.
Brothers, help to get her away from here, and I'll guard this door with my sword.
Follow, my lord, and I'll soon bring her back.
Follow, my lord, and I'll soon bring her back.
My lord, you pass not here.
My lord, you shall not pass here.
What, villain boy, / Barr'st me my way in Rome?
What, you villain boy, do you block my way in Rome?
My lord, you are unjust, and more than so, / In wrongful quarrel you have slain your son.
My lord, you are unjust, and worse than that: you have killed your son in a wrongful quarrel.
Nor thou nor he are any sons of mine; / My sons would never so dishonour me. / Traitor, restore Lavinia to the Emperor.
Neither you nor he is any son of mine. My sons would never dishonour me like this. Traitor, give Lavinia back to the emperor.
Dead, if you will; but not to be his wife, / That is another's lawful promised love.
Dead, if you like, but not to be his wife, when she is lawfully promised to another man.

No, Titus, no; the emperor needs her not, / Nor her, nor thee, nor any of thy stock. / I'll trust by leisure him that mocks me once; / Thee never, nor thy traitorous haughty sons, / Confederates all thus to dishonour me. / Was none in Rome to make a stale / But Saturnine? Full well, Andronicus, / Agree these deeds with that proud brag of thine / That said'st I begged the empire at thy hands.

No, Titus, no. The emperor does not need her, nor her, nor you, nor anyone of your family. I'll take my time before I trust a man who has made a fool of me once, and you I will never trust, nor your treacherous, arrogant sons, all plotting together to dishonour me. Was there no one in Rome to make a laughing stock of except Saturnine? These deeds fit very well, Andronicus, with your proud boast that I begged the empire from your hands.
O monstrous! What reproachful words are these?
Monstrous! What insulting words are these?

But go thy ways; go, give that changing piece / To him that flourished for her with his sword. / A valiant son-in-law thou shalt enjoy; / One fit to bandy with thy lawless sons, / To ruffle in the commonwealth of Rome.

But go on your way. Go, give that fickle piece of goods to the man who waved his sword to win her. You'll have a brave son-in-law, a fit one to brawl with your lawless sons and swagger about causing trouble in the state of Rome.
These words are razors to my wounded heart.
These words are razors to my wounded heart.

And therefore, lovely Tamora, Queen of Goths, / That like the stately Phœbe 'mongst her nymphs / Dost overshine the gallant'st dames of Rome, / If thou be pleased with this my sudden choice, / Behold, I choose thee, Tamora, for my bride, / And will create thee Empress of Rome. / Speak, Queen of Goths, dost thou applaud my choice? / And here I swear by all the Roman gods, / Sith priest and holy water are so near, / And tapers burn so bright, and everything / In readiness for Hymenæus stand, / I will not re-salute the streets of Rome, / Or climb my palace, till from forth this place / I lead espoused my bride along with me.

And so, lovely Tamora, Queen of the Goths, who outshine the finest ladies of Rome like the stately moon goddess among her nymphs: if you are pleased with this sudden choice of mine, look, I choose you, Tamora, to be my bride, and will make you Empress of Rome. Speak, Queen of the Goths, do you approve my choice? And here I swear by all the Roman gods, since the priest and holy water are so near, and the candles are burning so brightly, and everything stands ready for the god of marriage, that I will not greet the streets of Rome again or climb up to my palace until I lead my bride away from this place as my wife.
And here in sight of heaven to Rome I swear, / If Saturnine advance the Queen of Goths, / She will a handmaid be to his desires, / A loving nurse, a mother to his youth.
And here, in the sight of heaven, I swear to Rome that if Saturnine raises up the Queen of the Goths, she will be a servant to his wishes, a loving nurse, and a mother to his youth.

Ascend, fair queen, Pantheon. Lords, accompany / Your noble emperor and his lovely bride, / Sent by the heavens for Prince Saturnine, / Whose wisdom hath her fortune conquered. / There shall we consummate our spousal rites.

Fair queen, go up to the Pantheon. Lords, go with your noble emperor and his lovely bride, sent by the heavens for Prince Saturnine, who has wisely won her fortune for himself. There we will complete our marriage rites.
I am not bid to wait upon this bride. / Titus, when wert thou wont to walk alone, / Dishonoured thus, and challenged of wrongs?
I am not invited to attend this bride. Titus, when did you ever walk alone like this, dishonoured and accused of wrongs?
O Titus, see, O, see what thou hast done! / In a bad quarrel slain a virtuous son.
O Titus, look, look what you have done! You have killed a good son in a bad quarrel.
No, foolish tribune, no; no son of mine, / Nor thou, nor these, confederates in the deed / That hath dishonoured all our family. / Unworthy brother and unworthy sons!
No, foolish tribune, no. He's no son of mine, and neither are you, nor these, who joined together in the deed that has dishonoured our whole family. Unworthy brother and unworthy sons!
But let us give him burial, as becomes; / Give Mutius burial with our brethren.
But let us bury him properly. Let us bury Mutius with our brothers.

Traitors, away! He rests not in this tomb. / This monument five hundred years hath stood, / Which I have sumptuously re-edified. / Here none but soldiers and Rome's servitors / Repose in fame; none basely slain in brawls. / Bury him where you can, he comes not here.

Traitors, get away! He shall not rest in this tomb. This monument has stood for five hundred years, and I have rebuilt it at great cost. Here only soldiers and servants of Rome lie in glory, no one killed shamefully in a brawl. Bury him where you like; he is not coming in here.
My lord, this is impiety in you. / My nephew Mutius' deeds do plead for him; / He must be buried with his brethren.
My lord, this is a sin against the gods on your part. My nephew Mutius's deeds speak for him. He must be buried with his brothers.
And shall, or him we will accompany.
And he shall be, or we will go with him.
"And shall"? What villain was it spake that word?
'And he shall be'? What villain spoke those words?
He that would vouch it in any place but here.
One who would stand by them anywhere but here.
What, would you bury him in my despite?
What, would you bury him in spite of me?
No, noble Titus, but entreat of thee / To pardon Mutius and to bury him.
No, noble Titus, but we beg you to forgive Mutius and to bury him.
Marcus, even thou hast struck upon my crest, / And with these boys mine honour thou hast wounded. / My foes I do repute you every one; / So trouble me no more, but get you gone.
Marcus, even you have struck at my helmet, and with these boys you have wounded my honour. I count every one of you as my enemy. So trouble me no more, but go away.
He is not with himself; let us withdraw.
He is not himself. Let us leave.
Not I, till Mutius' bones be buried.
Not I, until Mutius's bones are buried.
Brother, for in that name doth nature plead,—
Brother, for nature pleads in that name—
Father, and in that name doth nature speak,—
Father, and nature speaks in that name—
Speak thou no more, if all the rest will speed.
Say no more, if the rest of you want to succeed.
Renowned Titus, more than half my soul,—
Famous Titus, more than half my soul—
Dear father, soul and substance of us all,—
Dear father, the soul and body of us all—

Suffer thy brother Marcus to inter / His noble nephew here in virtue's nest, / That died in honour and Lavinia's cause. / Thou art a Roman; be not barbarous. / The Greeks upon advice did bury Ajax, / That slew himself; and wise Laertes' son / Did graciously plead for his funerals. / Let not young Mutius, then, that was thy joy, / Be barred his entrance here.

Let your brother Marcus bury his noble nephew here, in this nest of virtue, since he died with honour and for Lavinia's cause. You are a Roman: do not be a barbarian. After due thought the Greeks buried Ajax, though he killed himself, and Ulysses, the wise son of Laertes, kindly argued for his funeral. Then do not let young Mutius, who was your joy, be shut out of here.
Rise, Marcus, rise. / The dismall'st day is this that e'er I saw, / To be dishonoured by my sons in Rome! / Well, bury him, and bury me the next.
Rise, Marcus, rise. This is the most miserable day I have ever seen: to be dishonoured by my own sons in Rome! Well, bury him, and bury me next.
There lie thy bones, sweet Mutius, with thy friends, / Till we with trophies do adorn thy tomb.
Lie there, sweet Mutius, with your loved ones, until we decorate your tomb with trophies.
[Kneeling] No man shed tears for noble Mutius; / He lives in fame that died in virtue's cause.
(Kneeling) Let no one shed tears for noble Mutius. He who died in the cause of virtue lives on in fame.
My lord, to step out of these dreary dumps, / How comes it that the subtle Queen of Goths / Is of a sudden thus advanced in Rome?
My lord, to come out of this gloom: how is it that the cunning Queen of the Goths has suddenly been raised so high in Rome?

I know not, Marcus, but I know it is. / Whether by device or no, the heavens can tell. / Is she not then beholding to the man / That brought her for this high good turn so far? / Yes, and will nobly him remunerate.

I don't know, Marcus, but I know it is so. Whether by scheming or not, heaven only knows. Isn't she in debt, then, to the man who brought her so far, to this great good fortune? Yes, and she will repay him nobly.
So, Bassianus, you have played your prize. / God give you joy, sir, of your gallant bride.
So, Bassianus, you have won your prize. God give you joy, sir, of your fine bride.
And you of yours, my lord. I say no more, / Nor wish no less; and so I take my leave.
And you of yours, my lord. I say no more, and wish no less, and so I take my leave.
Traitor, if Rome have law or we have power, / Thou and thy faction shall repent this rape.
Traitor, if Rome has laws or I have power, you and your party will regret this abduction.
Rape call you it, my lord, to seize my own, / My true betrothed love, and now my wife? / But let the laws of Rome determine all; / Meanwhile am I possessed of that is mine.
Do you call it abduction, my lord, to take what is mine, my true promised love and now my wife? But let the laws of Rome decide everything. Meanwhile I have what belongs to me.
'Tis good, sir. You are very short with us; / But if we live, we'll be as sharp with you.
Very well, sir. You are very curt with us, but if we live, we'll be just as sharp with you.

My lord, what I have done, as best I may, / Answer I must, and shall do with my life. / Only thus much I give your grace to know: / By all the duties that I owe to Rome, / This noble gentleman, Lord Titus here, / Is in opinion and in honour wronged, / That, in the rescue of Lavinia, / With his own hand did slay his youngest son, / In zeal to you, and highly moved to wrath / To be controlled in that he frankly gave. / Receive him then to favour, Saturnine, / That hath expressed himself in all his deeds / A father and a friend to thee and Rome.

My lord, I must answer for what I have done as best I can, and I will, with my life. I only want your grace to know this much: by all the duty I owe Rome, this noble gentleman, Lord Titus here, has been wronged in his reputation and his honour. To rescue Lavinia for you, he killed his youngest son with his own hand, out of loyalty to you, and furious at being thwarted in the gift he freely gave. So take him back into favour, Saturnine. In all his deeds he has shown himself a father and a friend to you and to Rome.
Prince Bassianus, leave to plead my deeds. / 'Tis thou, and those, that have dishonoured me. / Rome and the righteous heavens be my judge / How I have loved and honoured Saturnine.
Prince Bassianus, stop pleading on my behalf. It is you and these others who have dishonoured me. Let Rome and the just heavens judge how much I have loved and honoured Saturnine.
My worthy lord, if ever Tamora / Were gracious in those princely eyes of thine, / Then hear me speak indifferently for all; / And at my suit, sweet, pardon what is past.
My worthy lord, if Tamora was ever pleasing in those princely eyes of yours, then hear me speak fairly for all of them, and at my request, my sweet, forgive what is past.
What, madam, be dishonoured openly, / And basely put it up without revenge?
What, madam, be publicly dishonoured and meekly swallow it without revenge?

Not so, my lord; the gods of Rome forfend / I should be author to dishonour you! / But on mine honour dare I undertake / For good Lord Titus' innocence in all, / Whose fury not dissembled speaks his griefs. / Then at my suit look graciously on him; / Lose not so noble a friend on vain suppose, / Nor with sour looks afflict his gentle heart. / [Aside] My lord, be ruled by me, be won at last; / Dissemble all your griefs and discontents. / You are but newly planted in your throne; / Lest, then, the people, and patricians too, / Upon a just survey take Titus' part, / And so supplant you for ingratitude, / Which Rome reputes to be a heinous sin, / Yield at entreats, and then let me alone. / I'll find a day to massacre them all, / And raze their faction and their family, / The cruel father and his traitorous sons, / To whom I sued for my dear son's life; / And make them know what 'tis to let a queen / Kneel in the streets and beg for grace in vain. / [Aloud] Come, come, sweet emperor; come, Andronicus; / Take up this good old man, and cheer the heart / That dies in tempest of thy angry frown.

Not so, my lord. The gods of Rome forbid that I should be the cause of your dishonour! But I dare to vouch on my honour that good Lord Titus is innocent in all this. His fury, which he does not hide, shows how much he is grieving. So at my request look kindly on him. Do not lose so noble a friend over an empty suspicion, or hurt his gentle heart with sour looks. (Aside, to Saturninus) My lord, take my advice. Let yourself be won over at last. Hide all your grievances and resentment. You have only just been planted on your throne. In case the people, and the lords too, look carefully at the matter, take Titus's side, and overthrow you for ingratitude, which Rome thinks a terrible sin, give way to our pleading, and leave the rest to me. I'll find a day to massacre them all, and wipe out their party and their family: the cruel father and his treacherous sons, whom I begged for my dear son's life. I'll make them learn what it means to let a queen kneel in the streets and beg for mercy in vain. (Aloud) Come, come, sweet emperor. Come, Andronicus. Raise up this good old man, and cheer the heart that is dying in the storm of your angry frown.
Rise, Titus, rise; my empress hath prevailed.
Rise, Titus, rise. My empress has won me over.
I thank your majesty and her, my lord. / These words, these looks, infuse new life in me.
I thank your majesty, and her, my lord. These words and looks pour new life into me.

Titus, I am incorporate in Rome, / A Roman now adopted happily, / And must advise the emperor for his good. / This day all quarrels die, Andronicus; / And let it be mine honour, good my lord, / That I have reconciled your friends and you. / For you, Prince Bassianus, I have passed / My word and promise to the emperor / That you will be more mild and tractable. / And fear not, lords, and you, Lavinia. / By my advice, all humbled on your knees, / You shall ask pardon of his majesty.

Titus, I am now part of Rome, a Roman happily adopted, and I must advise the emperor for his own good. All quarrels die today, Andronicus. And let it be to my credit, my good lord, that I have reconciled your friends and you. As for you, Prince Bassianus, I have given my word and promise to the emperor that you will be gentler and more obedient. And do not be afraid, lords, nor you, Lavinia. On my advice, you shall all kneel humbly and ask his majesty's pardon.
We do, and vow to heaven and to his highness / That what we did was mildly as we might, / Tend'ring our sister's honour and our own.
We do, and we swear to heaven and to his highness that what we did was as gentle as we could make it, in protecting our sister's honour and our own.
That on mine honour here do I protest.
I swear to that here on my honour.
Away, and talk not; trouble us no more.
Go away, and say nothing. Don't trouble us any more.
Nay, nay, sweet emperor, we must all be friends. / The tribune and his nephews kneel for grace; / I will not be denied. Sweet heart, look back.
No, no, sweet emperor, we must all be friends. The tribune and his nephews are kneeling for pardon. I will not be refused. Sweetheart, look round.

Marcus, for thy sake, and thy brother's here, / And at my lovely Tamora's entreats, / I do remit these young men's heinous faults. / Stand up. / Lavinia, though you left me like a churl, / I found a friend, and sure as death I swore / I would not part a bachelor from the priest. / Come, if the emperor's court can feast two brides, / You are my guest, Lavinia, and your friends. / This day shall be a love-day, Tamora.

Marcus, for your sake, and your brother's here, and at the request of my lovely Tamora, I forgive these young men's terrible offences. Stand up. Lavinia, though you left me like a peasant, I found a friend, and I swore as surely as death that I would not leave the priest a bachelor. Come, if the emperor's court can feast two brides, you are my guest, Lavinia, and your friends too. This shall be a day of reconciliation, Tamora.
Tomorrow, an it please your majesty / To hunt the panther and the hart with me, / With horn and hound we'll give your grace bonjour.
Tomorrow, if your majesty would like to hunt the panther and the deer with me, we'll wish your grace good morning with horn and hound.
Be it so, Titus, and gramercy too.
So be it, Titus, and many thanks.

Now climbeth Tamora Olympus' top, / Safe out of Fortune's shot, and sits aloft, / Secure of thunder's crack or lightning's flash, / Advanced above pale envy's threat'ning reach. / As when the golden sun salutes the morn, / And, having gilt the ocean with his beams, / Gallops the zodiac in his glistening coach, / And overlooks the highest-peering hills; / So Tamora. / Upon her wit doth earthly honour wait, / And virtue stoops and trembles at her frown. / Then, Aaron, arm thy heart and fit thy thoughts / To mount aloft with thy imperial mistress, / And mount her pitch, whom thou in triumph long / Hast prisoner held, fett'red in amorous chains, / And faster bound to Aaron's charming eyes / Than is Prometheus tied to Caucasus. / Away with slavish weeds and servile thoughts! / I will be bright, and shine in pearl and gold, / To wait upon this new-made empress. / To wait, said I? To wanton with this queen, / This goddess, this Semiramis, this nymph, / This siren, that will charm Rome's Saturnine, / And see his shipwrack and his commonweal's. / Holla! What storm is this?

Now Tamora climbs to the top of Olympus, safe from Fortune's arrows, and sits up high, out of reach of the crack of thunder or the flash of lightning, raised above the threatening reach of pale envy. Just as the golden sun greets the morning, gilds the ocean with its rays, gallops through the zodiac in its glittering chariot and looks down on the highest hills: so does Tamora. Earthly honour waits on her intelligence, and virtue bows and trembles when she frowns. Then, Aaron, steel your heart and shape your thoughts to rise high with your imperial mistress. Rise to her height, she whom you have long held prisoner in triumph, chained in the chains of love, and bound faster to Aaron's charming eyes than Prometheus is chained to the Caucasus. Away with the clothes and thoughts of a slave! I will be splendid, and shine in pearl and gold, to serve this new-made empress. Serve, did I say? To play with this queen, this goddess, this Semiramis, this nymph, this siren, who will bewitch Rome's Saturnine and watch him and his state wrecked. Hello! What storm is this?
Chiron, thy years wants wit, thy wit wants edge / And manners, to intrude where I am graced, / And may, for aught thou knowest, affected be.
Chiron, you are too young to have any sense, and your sense has no sharpness and no manners, if you push in where I am in favour, and may be loved, for all you know.

Demetrius, thou dost overween in all, / And so in this, to bear me down with braves. / 'Tis not the difference of a year or two / Makes me less gracious or thee more fortunate. / I am as able and as fit as thou / To serve and to deserve my mistress' grace; / And that my sword upon thee shall approve, / And plead my passions for Lavinia's love.

Demetrius, you are arrogant about everything, and so you are about this, trying to crush me with threats. A year or two's difference in age doesn't make me less attractive or you more lucky. I am as able and as fit as you are to serve my mistress and to deserve her favour, and my sword shall prove it on you and argue my passion for Lavinia's love.
[Aside] Clubs, clubs! These lovers will not keep the peace.
(Aside) Break it up! These lovers will not keep the peace.

Why, boy, although our mother, unadvised, / Gave you a dancing-rapier by your side, / Are you so desperate grown to threat your friends? / Go to; have your lath glued within your sheath / Till you know better how to handle it.

Why, boy, just because our mother foolishly gave you a dancing sword to wear at your side, have you grown so reckless that you threaten your own family? Get away. Have your wooden toy glued into its sheath until you know better how to use it.
Meanwhile, sir, with the little skill I have, / Full well shalt thou perceive how much I dare.
Meanwhile, sir, with the little skill I have, you'll soon see how much I dare.
Ay, boy, grow ye so brave?
Yes, boy, are you so brave now?

Why, how now, lords! / So near the emperor's palace dare ye draw, / And maintain such a quarrel openly? / Full well I wot the ground of all this grudge. / I would not for a million of gold / The cause were known to them it most concerns; / Nor would your noble mother for much more / Be so dishonoured in the court of Rome. / For shame, put up.

Why, what's this, lords! Do you dare to draw your swords so near the emperor's palace and keep up a quarrel like this in the open? I know very well what this feud is about. I wouldn't have the cause known to the people it most concerns for a million in gold, and your noble mother would not be so dishonoured in the court of Rome for much more. For shame, put your swords away.
Not I, till I have sheathed / My rapier in his bosom, and withal / Thrust those reproachful speeches down his throat / That he hath breathed in my dishonour here.
Not I, until I have sheathed my sword in his chest, and with it rammed those insults he has spoken against my honour down his throat.
For that I am prepared and full resolved, / Foul-spoken coward, that thund'rest with thy tongue, / And with thy weapon nothing dar'st perform.
I am ready and fully determined for that, you foul-mouthed coward, who thunder with your tongue and dare do nothing with your weapon.

Away, I say! / Now, by the gods that warlike Goths adore, / This pretty brabble will undo us all. / Why, lords, and think you not how dangerous / It is to jet upon a prince's right? / What, is Lavinia then become so loose, / Or Bassianus so degenerate, / That for her love such quarrels may be broached / Without controlment, justice, or revenge? / Young lords, beware! And should the empress know / This discord's ground, the music would not please.

Get apart, I say! Now, by the gods the warlike Goths worship, this silly squabble will ruin us all. Why, lords, don't you see how dangerous it is to trespass on a prince's rights? What, has Lavinia become so loose, or Bassianus so feeble, that quarrels can be started over her love without restraint, justice or revenge? Young lords, be careful! If the empress knew the cause of this discord, the tune would not please her.
I care not, I, knew she and all the world. / I love Lavinia more than all the world.
I don't care if she and all the world knew it. I love Lavinia more than all the world.
Youngling, learn thou to make some meaner choice. / Lavina is thine elder brother's hope.
Youngster, learn to make a humbler choice. Lavinia is your elder brother's hope.
Why, are ye mad? Or know ye not in Rome / How furious and impatient they be, / And cannot brook competitors in love? / I tell you, lords, you do but plot your deaths / By this device.
Why, are you mad? Don't you know how fierce and hot-tempered they are in Rome, and how they cannot stand rivals in love? I tell you, lords, with this plan you are only plotting your own deaths.
Aaron, a thousand deaths / Would I propose to achieve her whom I love.
Aaron, I would face a thousand deaths to win the woman I love.

Why makes thou it so strange? / She is a woman, therefore may be wooed; / She is a woman, therefore may be won; / She is Lavinia, therefore must be loved. / What, man, more water glideth by the mill / Than wots the miller of; and easy it is / Of a cut loaf to steal a shive, we know. / Though Bassianus be the emperor's brother, / Better than he have worn Vulcan's badge.

Why are you so surprised? She is a woman, so she may be wooed. She is a woman, so she may be won. She is Lavinia, so she must be loved. What, man, more water slides past the mill than the miller knows about, and it's easy, we know, to steal a slice from a loaf that has already been cut. Though Bassianus is the emperor's brother, better men than he have worn the cuckold's horns.
[Aside] Ay, and as good as Saturninus may.
(Aside) Yes, and men as good as Saturninus may too.
Then why should he despair that knows to court it / With words, fair looks, and liberality? / What, hast not thou full often struck a doe, / And borne her cleanly by the keeper's nose?
Then why should a man despair, if he knows how to court a woman with words, good looks and generous gifts? What, haven't you often shot a deer and carried her off neatly under the gamekeeper's nose?
Why, then, it seems some certain snatch or so / Would serve your turns.
Why, then it seems a quick grab or something like it would serve your purpose.
Ay, so the turn were served.
Yes, if the purpose were served.
Would you had hit it too! / Then should not we be tired with this ado. / Why, hark ye, hark ye, and are you such fools / To square for this? Would it offend you then / That both should speed?
I wish you had hit it too! Then we wouldn't be wearied with all this fuss. Why, listen, listen, are you such fools as to fight over this? Would it offend you if you both succeeded?
Nor me, so I were one.
Nor me, as long as I was one of them.

For shame, be friends, and join for that you jar. / 'Tis policy and stratagem must do / That you affect; and so must you resolve / That what you cannot as you would achieve, / You must perforce accomplish as you may. / Take this of me: Lucrece was not more chaste / Than this Lavinia, Bassianus' love. / A speedier course than ling'ring languishment / Must we pursue, and I have found the path. / My lords, a solemn hunting is in hand; / There will the lovely Roman ladies troop. / The forest walks are wide and spacious, / And many unfrequented plots there are / Fitted by kind for rape and villainy. / Single you thither, then, this dainty doe, / And strike her home by force, if not by words. / This way, or not at all, stand you in hope. / Come, come, our empress, with her sacred wit / To villainy and vengeance consecrate, / Will we acquaint with all what we intend; / And she shall file our engines with advice / That will not suffer you to square yourselves, / But to your wishes' height advance you both. / The emperor's court is like the house of Fame, / The palace full of tongues, of eyes and ears; / The woods are ruthless, dreadful, deaf, and dull. / There speak and strike, brave boys, and take your turns; / There serve your lust, shadowed from heaven's eye, / And revel in Lavinia's treasury.

For shame, be friends, and join together for what you are quarrelling over. Cunning and strategy must get you what you want. You must make up your minds that what you cannot achieve the way you would like, you must achieve however you can. Take it from me: Lucrece was not more chaste than this Lavinia, Bassianus's love. We must take a quicker route than lingering lovesickness, and I have found the way. My lords, a grand hunt is being planned. The lovely Roman ladies will flock there. The forest paths are wide and roomy, and there are many lonely places that nature has made fit for rape and villainy. Pick out this dainty doe there, then, and bring her down by force if not by words. This way, or not at all, is your hope. Come, come, we will tell our empress everything we intend. Her mind is devoted to villainy and revenge, and she will sharpen our plans with advice that will stop you fighting each other and lift you both to the height of your wishes. The emperor's court is like the House of Rumour: the palace is full of tongues, eyes and ears. The woods are pitiless, dreadful, deaf and silent. There, brave boys, speak and strike and take your turns. There satisfy your lust, hidden from heaven's eye, and feast on Lavinia's treasure.
Thy counsel, lad, smells of no cowardice.
Your advice, lad, doesn't smell of cowardice.
Sit fas aut nefas, till I find the stream / To cool this heat, a charm to calm these fits, / Per Stygia, per manes vehor.
Right or wrong, until I find the stream to cool this heat and a spell to calm these fits, I am carried through the Styx and among the ghosts of the dead.

The hunt is up, the morn is bright and grey, / The fields are fragrant, and the woods are green. / Uncouple here, and let us make a bay, / And wake the emperor and his lovely bride, / And rouse the prince, and ring a hunter's peal, / That all the court may echo with the noise. / Sons, let it be your charge, as it is ours, / To attend the emperor's person carefully. / I have been troubled in my sleep this night, / But dawning day new comfort hath inspired.

The hunt is on, the morning is bright and grey, the fields smell sweet and the woods are green. Let the hounds loose here, and let us make them bark, and wake the emperor and his lovely bride, and rouse the prince, and ring out a hunting peal so the whole court echoes with the noise. Sons, make it your duty, as it is ours, to look after the emperor's person carefully. My sleep was troubled last night, but the dawning day has given me new comfort.
Many good morrows to your majesty; / Madam, to you as many and as good. / I promised your grace a hunter's peal.
Many good mornings to your majesty. Madam, as many to you, and just as good. I promised your grace a hunting peal.
And you have rung it lustily, my lords; / Somewhat too early for new-married ladies.
And you have rung it heartily, my lords: a little too early for newly married ladies.
I say no; / I have been broad awake two hours and more.
I say no. I have been wide awake for more than two hours.
Come on then; horse and chariots let us have, / And to our sport. [To Tamora] Madam, now shall ye see / Our Roman hunting.
Come on, then. Let's have horses and chariots, and off to our sport. (To Tamora) Madam, now you shall see our Roman hunting.
I have dogs, my lord, / Will rouse the proudest panther in the chase, / And climb the highest promontory top.
I have dogs, my lord, that will flush out the proudest panther in the hunt and climb to the top of the highest cliff.
And I have horse will follow where the game / Makes way, and run like swallows o'er the plain.
And I have horses that will follow wherever the game runs, and race across the plain like swallows.
Chiron, we hunt not, we, with horse nor hound, / But hope to pluck a dainty doe to ground.
Chiron, we are not hunting with horse or hound, but hoping to pull a dainty doe to the ground.

He that had wit would think that I had none, / To bury so much gold under a tree, / And never after to inherit it. / Let him that thinks of me so abjectly / Know that this gold must coin a stratagem, / Which, cunningly effected, will beget / A very excellent piece of villainy. / And so repose, sweet gold, for their unrest / That have their alms out of the empress' chest.

A clever man would think I had no sense, burying so much gold under a tree and never getting to enjoy it afterwards. Let anyone who thinks so poorly of me know that this gold must mint a scheme which, carried out cunningly, will produce a really excellent piece of villainy. So rest, sweet gold, to bring trouble on those who get their charity out of the empress's purse.

My lovely Aaron, wherefore look'st thou sad / When everything doth make a gleeful boast? / The birds chant melody on every bush, / The snakes lie rolled in the cheerful sun, / The green leaves quiver with the cooling wind, / And make a chequered shadow on the ground. / Under their sweet shade, Aaron, let us sit, / And whilst the babbling echo mocks the hounds, / Replying shrilly to the well-tuned horns, / As if a double hunt were heard at once, / Let us sit down and mark their yelping noise; / And after conflict such as was supposed / The wand'ring prince and Dido once enjoyed, / When with a happy storm they were surprised, / And curtained with a counsel-keeping cave, / We may, each wreathed in the other's arms, / Our pastimes done, possess a golden slumber, / Whiles hounds and horns and sweet melodious birds / Be unto us as is a nurse's song / Of lullaby to bring her babe asleep.

My lovely Aaron, why do you look sad when everything is showing off its happiness? The birds sing on every bush, the snakes lie coiled in the cheerful sun, the green leaves quiver in the cool breeze and make a chequered shadow on the ground. Let us sit in their sweet shade, Aaron, and while the chattering echo mocks the hounds, answering the tuneful horns so shrilly that it sounds like two hunts at once, let us sit and listen to their yelping. And after a struggle like the one the wandering prince Aeneas and Dido are said to have enjoyed, when a lucky storm caught them and they were hidden in a cave that kept their secret, we may lie wrapped in each other's arms, our games over, and fall into a golden sleep, while hounds and horns and sweet singing birds are to us like a nurse's lullaby that sends her baby to sleep.

Madam, though Venus govern your desires, / Saturn is dominator over mine. / What signifies my deadly-standing eye, / My silence and my cloudy melancholy, / My fleece of woolly hair that now uncurls / Even as an adder when she doth unroll / To do some fatal execution? / No, madam, these are no venereal signs. / Vengeance is in my heart, death in my hand, / Blood and revenge are hammering in my head. / Hark, Tamora, the empress of my soul, / Which never hopes more heaven than rests in thee, / This is the day of doom for Bassianus; / His Philomel must lose her tongue today, / Thy sons make pillage of her chastity, / And wash their hands in Bassianus' blood. / Seest thou this letter? Take it up, I pray thee, / And give the king this fatal-plotted scroll. / Now question me no more; we are espied; / Here comes a parcel of our hopeful booty, / Which dreads not yet their lives' destruction.

Madam, though Venus rules your desires, Saturn rules mine. What do you think my deadly fixed stare means, my silence and my gloomy melancholy, my fleece of woolly hair uncurling like an adder unrolling to make a fatal strike? No, madam, these are not signs of love. Vengeance is in my heart and death in my hand. Blood and revenge are hammering in my head. Listen, Tamora, empress of my soul, which hopes for no more heaven than it finds in you: this is the day of doom for Bassianus. His Philomel must lose her tongue today. Your sons will plunder her chastity and wash their hands in Bassianus's blood. Do you see this letter? Please pick it up and give the king this deadly scroll. Now ask me nothing more. We are being watched. Here comes some of the loot we are hoping for, and they have no idea their lives are about to be destroyed.
Ah, my sweet Moor, sweeter to me than life!
Ah, my sweet Moor, sweeter to me than life!
No more, great empress. Bassianus comes. / Be cross with him; and I'll go fetch thy sons / To back thy quarrels, whatsoe'er they be.
No more, great empress. Bassianus is coming. Pick a quarrel with him, and I'll go and fetch your sons to support you, whatever the quarrel is.
Who have we here? Rome's royal empress, / Unfurnished of her well-beseeming troop? / Or is it Dian, habited like her, / Who hath abandoned her holy groves / To see the general hunting in this forest?
Who is this? Rome's royal empress, without her proper company? Or is it Diana, dressed like her, who has left her holy groves to watch the public hunt in this forest?

Saucy controller of my private steps! / Had I the power that some say Dian had, / Thy temples should be planted presently / With horns, as was Actaeon's; and the hounds / Should drive upon thy new-transformed limbs, / Unmannerly intruder as thou art.

You insolent spy on my private walks! If I had the power some say Diana had, your forehead would sprout horns at once, like Actaeon's, and the hounds would leap on your newly transformed body, rude intruder that you are.

Under your patience, gentle empress, / 'Tis thought you have a goodly gift in horning, / And to be doubted that your Moor and you / Are singled forth to try experiments. / Jove shield your husband from his hounds today! / 'Tis pity they should take him for a stag.

With respect, gentle empress, people think you have a fine talent for giving men horns, and it is suspected that you and your Moor have gone off alone to try some experiments. Jove protect your husband from his hounds today! It would be a pity if they took him for a stag.

Believe me, queen, your swarthy Cimmerian / Doth make your honour of his body's hue, / Spotted, detested, and abominable. / Why are you sequestered from all your train, / Dismounted from your snow-white goodly steed, / And wandered hither to an obscure plot, / Accompanied but with a barbarous Moor, / If foul desire had not conducted you?

Believe me, queen, your dark-skinned Cimmerian is making your honour the colour of his body: stained, hated and disgusting. Why are you separated from all your attendants, off your fine snow-white horse, and wandering in this hidden spot with no one but a barbarous Moor, unless foul desire led you here?

And, being intercepted in your sport, / Great reason that my noble lord be rated / For sauciness. I pray you, let us hence, / And let her joy her raven-coloured love; / This valley fits the purpose passing well.

And since we have interrupted your sport, there is good reason to scold my noble lord for his rudeness. Please, let's go, and let her enjoy her raven-coloured love. This valley suits the purpose extremely well.
The king my brother shall have notice of this.
The king my brother shall hear about this.
Ay, for these slips have made him noted long. / Good king, to be so mightily abused!
Yes, these slips have made him notorious for a long time. Good king, to be so badly deceived!
Why, I have patience to endure all this.
Why, I have patience to put up with all this.
How now, dear sovereign, and our gracious mother! / Why doth your highness look so pale and wan?
What's the matter, dear sovereign and our gracious mother? Why does your highness look so pale and drained?

Have I not reason, think you, to look pale? / These two have ticed me hither to this place, / A barren detested vale you see it is; / The trees, though summer, yet forlorn and lean, / Overcome with moss and baleful mistletoe. / Here never shines the sun, here nothing breeds, / Unless the nightly owl or fatal raven. / And when they showed me this abhorred pit, / They told me, here, at dead time of the night, / A thousand fiends, a thousand hissing snakes, / Ten thousand swelling toads, as many urchins, / Would make such fearful and confused cries / As any mortal body hearing it / Should straight fall mad, or else die suddenly. / No sooner had they told this hellish tale / But straight they told me they would bind me here / Unto the body of a dismal yew, / And leave me to this miserable death. / And then they called me foul adulteress, / Lascivious Goth, and all the bitterest terms / That ever ear did hear to such effect. / And had you not by wondrous fortune come, / This vengeance on me had they executed. / Revenge it, as you love your mother's life, / Or be ye not henceforth called my children.

Don't you think I have reason to look pale? These two lured me here to this place. You can see it is a barren, hateful valley. The trees, though it is summer, are bare and thin, smothered in moss and deadly mistletoe. The sun never shines here, nothing breeds here, except the owl of the night and the raven of death. And when they showed me this horrible pit, they told me that here, in the dead of night, a thousand devils, a thousand hissing snakes, ten thousand swelling toads and as many hedgehogs make such terrifying, confused cries that any living person who hears them would go mad at once or die suddenly. As soon as they had told this hellish story, they told me they would tie me here to the trunk of a gloomy yew tree and leave me to this miserable death. And then they called me a foul adulteress, a lustful Goth, and all the bitterest names ever heard of that kind. If you had not come here by wonderful luck, they would have carried out this vengeance on me. Revenge it, if you love your mother's life, or never call yourselves my children again.
This is a witness that I am thy son.
This is proof that I am your son.
And this for me, struck home to show my strength.
And this is for me, struck deep to show my strength.
Ay, come, Semiramis, nay, barbarous Tamora, / For no name fits thy nature but thy own!
Yes, come, Semiramis, no, barbarous Tamora, for no name fits your nature but your own!
Give me thy poniard; you shall know, my boys, / Your mother's hand shall right your mother's wrong.
Give me your dagger. You shall see, my boys, that your mother's hand will avenge your mother's wrong.

Stay, madam, here is more belongs to her. / First thrash the corn, then after burn the straw. / This minion stood upon her chastity, / Upon her nuptial vow, her loyalty, / And with that painted hope braves your mightiness; / And shall she carry this unto her grave?

Wait, madam, there is more owed to her. First thresh the corn, then burn the straw. This little madam made a great deal of her chastity, her marriage vow and her loyalty, and with that pretty show she defies your greatness. Shall she carry it with her to the grave?
And if she do, I would I were an eunuch. / Drag hence her husband to some secret hole, / And make his dead trunk pillow to our lust.
If she does, I wish I were a eunuch. Drag her husband away to some hidden hole, and make his dead body a pillow for our lust.
But when ye have the honey ye desire, / Let not this wasp outlive, us both to sting.
But when you have the honey you want, do not let this wasp live on to sting us both.
I warrant you, madam, we will make that sure. / Come, mistress, now perforce we will enjoy / That nice-preserved honesty of yours.
I promise you, madam, we will make sure of that. Come, mistress, now we will enjoy by force that carefully guarded chastity of yours.
O Tamora, thou bearest a woman's face,—
O Tamora, you have a woman's face—
I will not hear her speak; away with her!
I won't hear her speak. Take her away!
Sweet lords, entreat her hear me but a word.
Sweet lords, beg her to hear just one word from me.
Listen, fair madam: let it be your glory / To see her tears; but be your heart to them / As unrelenting flint to drops of rain.
Listen, fair madam. Let it be your glory to see her tears, but let your heart be to them as hard as flint is to drops of rain.

When did the tiger's young ones teach the dam? / O, do not learn her wrath; she taught it thee; / The milk thou suck'st from her did turn to marble; / Even at thy teat thou hadst thy tyranny. / Yet every mother breeds not sons alike. / [To Chiron] Do thou entreat her show a woman's pity.

When did a tiger's cubs ever teach their mother? O, don't learn anger from her: she taught it to you. The milk you sucked from her turned to marble. You got your cruelty at her breast. Yet not every mother has sons who are alike. (To Chiron) You beg her to show a woman's pity.
What, wouldst thou have me prove myself a bastard?
What, would you have me prove I'm a bastard?

'Tis true the raven doth not hatch a lark. / Yet have I heard—O, could I find it now!— / The lion, moved with pity, did endure / To have his princely paws pared all away. / Some say that ravens foster forlorn children, / The whilst their own birds famish in their nests. / O, be to me, though thy hard heart say no, / Nothing so kind, but something pitiful.

It's true a raven does not hatch a lark. Yet I have heard (O, if only I could find it true now!) that a lion, moved by pity, let his royal claws be clipped away. Some say ravens feed abandoned children while their own young starve in the nest. O, though your hard heart says no, be, not so kind to me, but just a little merciful.
I know not what it means; away with her!
I don't know what that means. Take her away!
O, let me teach thee! For my father's sake, / That gave thee life when well he might have slain thee, / Be not obdurate, open thy deaf ears.
O, let me teach you! For the sake of my father, who spared your life when he could easily have killed you, don't be so hard. Open your deaf ears.

Hadst thou in person ne'er offended me, / Even for his sake am I pitiless. / Remember, boys, I poured forth tears in vain / To save your brother from the sacrifice, / But fierce Andronicus would not relent. / Therefore away with her, and use her as you will; / The worse to her, the better loved of me.

Even if you had never offended me yourself, I would be pitiless for his sake. Remember, boys, I poured out tears in vain to save your brother from the sacrifice, but fierce Andronicus would not give way. So take her away, and do what you like with her. The worse for her, the more I'll love you.
O Tamora, be called a gentle queen, / And with thine own hands kill me in this place! / For 'tis not life that I have begged so long; / Poor I was slain when Bassianus died.
O Tamora, earn the name of a gentle queen, and kill me here with your own hands! For it is not life I have been begging for all this time. Poor me, I died when Bassianus died.
What begg'st thou, then? Fond woman, let me go.
What are you begging for, then? Foolish woman, let me go.

'Tis present death I beg; and one thing more / That womanhood denies my tongue to tell. / O, keep me from their worse than killing lust, / And tumble me into some loathsome pit, / Where never man's eye may behold my body. / Do this, and be a charitable murderer.

It is instant death I beg for, and one thing more that my modesty will not let my tongue name. O, save me from their lust, which is worse than killing, and throw me into some foul pit where no man will ever see my body. Do this, and be a merciful murderer.
So should I rob my sweet sons of their fee. / No, let them satisfy their lust on thee.
Then I'd be robbing my sweet sons of their reward. No, let them satisfy their lust on you.
Away, for thou hast stayed us here too long.
Come on, you have kept us here too long.
No grace, no womanhood? Ah, beastly creature, / The blot and enemy to our general name! / Confusion fall—
No grace, no womanhood? Ah, you beastly creature, the shame and enemy of all women! May destruction fall—
Nay, then I'll stop your mouth. Bring thou her husband. / This is the hole where Aaron bid us hide him.
No, then I'll stop your mouth. You bring her husband. This is the hole where Aaron told us to hide him.

Farewell, my sons. See that you make her sure. / Ne'er let my heart know merry cheer indeed / Till all the Andronici be made away. / Now will I hence to seek my lovely Moor, / And let my spleenful sons this trull deflower.
Farewell, my sons. Make sure of her. My heart will never know real happiness until all the Andronici are done away with. Now I'll go and find my lovely Moor, and let my angry sons rape this whore.
Come on, my lords, the better foot before. / Straight will I bring you to the loathsome pit / Where I espied the panther fast asleep.
Come on, my lords, best foot forward. I'll take you straight to the horrible pit where I saw the panther fast asleep.
My sight is very dull, whate'er it bodes.
My eyes are very heavy, whatever that means.
And mine, I promise you. Were it not for shame, / Well could I leave our sport to sleep awhile.
Mine too, I promise you. If it weren't shameful, I could happily leave the hunt and sleep for a while.

What, art thou fallen? What subtle hole is this, / Whose mouth is covered with rude-growing briers, / Upon whose leaves are drops of new-shed blood / As fresh as morning dew distilled on flowers? / A very fatal place it seems to me. / Speak, brother, hast thou hurt thee with the fall?

What, have you fallen? What hidden hole is this, its mouth covered with wild-growing brambles, with drops of freshly spilt blood on their leaves, as fresh as morning dew on flowers? It seems a deadly place to me. Speak, brother, have you hurt yourself in the fall?
O brother, with the dismall'st object hurt / That ever eye with sight made heart lament!
O brother, I am hurt by the most dreadful sight that ever made a heart grieve!
[Aside] Now will I fetch the king to find them here, / That he thereby may have a likely guess / How these were they that made away his brother.
(Aside) Now I'll fetch the king to find them here, so that he can make a likely guess that these are the ones who killed his brother.
Why dost not comfort me, and help me out / From this unhallowed and blood-stained hole?
Why don't you comfort me and help me out of this unholy, bloodstained hole?
I am surprised with an uncouth fear; / A chilling sweat o'er-runs my trembling joints. / My heart suspects more than mine eye can see.
I am gripped by a strange fear. A cold sweat runs over my trembling limbs. My heart suspects more than my eyes can see.
To prove thou hast a true-divining heart, / Aaron and thou look down into this den, / And see a fearful sight of blood and death.
To prove your heart has guessed right, you and Aaron look down into this den, and see a terrible sight of blood and death.

Aaron is gone, and my compassionate heart / Will not permit mine eyes once to behold / The thing whereat it trembles by surmise. / O, tell me who it is; for ne'er till now / Was I a child to fear I know not what.
Aaron has gone, and my pitying heart will not let my eyes look at the thing it trembles to imagine. O, tell me who it is, for until now I was never so childish as to be afraid of I don't know what.
Lord Bassianus lies berayed in blood, / All on a heap, like to a slaughtered lamb, / In this detested, dark, blood-drinking pit.
Lord Bassianus lies here smeared in blood, all in a heap like a slaughtered lamb, in this hateful, dark, blood-drinking pit.
If it be dark, how dost thou know 'tis he?
If it's dark, how do you know it's him?

Upon his bloody finger he doth wear / A precious ring that lightens all the hole, / Which, like a taper in some monument, / Doth shine upon the dead man's earthy cheeks, / And shows the ragged entrails of the pit. / So pale did shine the moon on Pyramus / When he by night lay bathed in maiden blood. / O brother, help me with thy fainting hand, / If fear hath made thee faint, as me it hath, / Out of this fell devouring receptacle, / As hateful as Cocytus' misty mouth.

On his bloody finger he wears a precious ring that lights up the whole hole. Like a candle in a tomb, it shines on the dead man's earthy cheeks and shows the jagged insides of the pit. The moon shone just as pale on Pyramus when he lay at night bathed in a maiden's blood. O brother, if fear has made you faint, as it has me, help me with your fainting hand out of this cruel, devouring hole, as hateful as the misty mouth of the river Cocytus in hell.

Reach me thy hand, that I may help thee out, / Or, wanting strength to do thee so much good, / I may be plucked into the swallowing womb / Of this deep pit, poor Bassianus' grave. / I have no strength to pluck thee to the brink.

Give me your hand so that I can help you out, or, if I haven't the strength to do you that much good, be pulled down myself into the swallowing belly of this deep pit, poor Bassianus's grave. I haven't the strength to pull you to the edge.
Nor I no strength to climb without thy help.
And I haven't the strength to climb out without your help.
Thy hand once more; I will not loose again, / Till thou art here aloft, or I below. / Thou canst not come to me. I come to thee.
Your hand once more. I won't let go again until you are up here or I am down there. You can't come to me: I'll come to you.
Along with me! I'll see what hole is here, / And what he is that now is leapt into it. / Say, who art thou that lately didst descend / Into this gaping hollow of the earth?
Come with me! I'll see what hole this is, and who it is that has just jumped into it. Tell me, who are you who just went down into this gaping hollow in the earth?
The unhappy sons of old Andronicus, / Brought hither in a most unlucky hour, / To find thy brother Bassianus dead.
The unlucky sons of old Andronicus, brought here at a most unlucky hour to find your brother Bassianus dead.
My brother dead! I know thou dost but jest. / He and his lady both are at the lodge / Upon the north side of this pleasant chase; / 'Tis not an hour since I left them there.
My brother dead! I know you are only joking. He and his lady are both at the lodge on the north side of this pleasant hunting ground. I left them there less than an hour ago.
We know not where you left them all alive; / But, out, alas, here have we found him dead.
We don't know where you left them alive, but, alas, we have found him dead here.
Where is my lord the king?
Where is my lord the king?
Here, Tamora; though grieved with killing grief.
Here, Tamora, though stricken with a killing grief.
Now to the bottom dost thou search my wound. / Poor Bassianus here lies murdered.
Now you are probing to the bottom of my wound. Poor Bassianus lies here murdered.
Then all too late I bring this fatal writ, / The complot of this timeless tragedy; / And wonder greatly that man's face can fold / In pleasing smiles such murderous tyranny.
Then I bring this deadly letter far too late: the plot of this untimely tragedy. And I am amazed that a man's face can hide such murderous cruelty behind pleasant smiles.
