[Reads] An if we miss to meet him handsomely, / Sweet huntsman, Bassianus 'tis we mean, / Do thou so much as dig the grave for him; / Thou know'st our meaning. Look for thy reward / Among the nettles at the elder-tree / Which overshades the mouth of that same pit / Where we decreed to bury Bassianus. / Do this, and purchase us thy lasting friends. / O Tamora, was ever heard the like? / This is the pit, and this the elder-tree. / Look, sirs, if you can find the huntsman out / That should have murdered Bassianus here.

(Reads) 'If we fail to catch him neatly, sweet huntsman (it's Bassianus we mean), you just dig the grave for him. You know what we mean. Look for your reward among the nettles at the elder tree which overhangs the mouth of the same pit where we decided to bury Bassianus. Do this, and make us your friends for ever.' O Tamora, did anyone ever hear the like? This is the pit, and this is the elder tree. Look, sirs, and see if you can find the huntsman who was meant to murder Bassianus here.
My gracious lord, here is the bag of gold.
My gracious lord, here is the bag of gold.

[To Titus] Two of thy whelps, fell curs of bloody kind, / Have here bereft my brother of his life. / Sirs, drag them from the pit unto the prison. / There let them bide until we have devised / Some never-heard-of torturing pain for them.

(To Titus) Two of your puppies, savage curs of a bloody breed, have taken my brother's life here. Sirs, drag them from the pit to prison. Let them stay there until we have thought up some never-heard-of torture for them.
What, are they in this pit? O wondrous thing! / How easily murder is discovered!
What, are they in this pit? How amazing! How easily murder comes to light!
High emperor, upon my feeble knee / I beg this boon, with tears not lightly shed, / That this fell fault of my accursed sons, / Accursed if the fault be proved in them—
Mighty emperor, on my weak knee I beg this favour, with tears not easily shed: that this cruel crime of my cursed sons, cursed if the crime is proved against them—
If it be proved! You see it is apparent. / Who found this letter? Tamora, was it you?
If it's proved! You can see it is obvious. Who found this letter? Tamora, was it you?
Andronicus himself did take it up.
I did, my lord, yet let me be their bail; / For by my fathers' reverend tomb I vow / They shall be ready at your highness' will / To answer their suspicion with their lives.
I did, my lord, yet let me stand bail for them. For I swear by my fathers' sacred tomb that they will be ready whenever your highness wishes to answer the suspicion with their lives.

Thou shalt not bail them. See thou follow me. / Some bring the murdered body, some the murderers. / Let them not speak a word; the guilt is plain; / For, by my soul, were there worse end than death, / That end upon them should be executed.

You shall not stand bail for them. Make sure you follow me. Some of you bring the murdered body, some the murderers. Don't let them speak a word: the guilt is plain. For, by my soul, if there were a worse end than death, they would suffer it.
Andronicus, I will entreat the king. / Fear not thy sons; they shall do well enough.
Andronicus, I will plead with the king. Don't worry about your sons; they'll be all right.
Come, Lucius, come; stay not to talk with them.
Come, Lucius, come. Don't stay to talk with them.
So, now go tell, an if thy tongue can speak, / Who 'twas that cut thy tongue and ravished thee.
So, now go and tell, if your tongue can speak, who it was that cut out your tongue and raped you.
Write down thy mind, bewray thy meaning so, / An if thy stumps will let thee play the scribe.
Write down your thoughts and reveal your meaning that way, if your stumps will let you play the writer.
See how with signs and tokens she can scrowl.
See how she can scrawl with signs and gestures.
Go home, call for sweet water, wash thy hands.
Go home, call for scented water, and wash your hands.
She hath no tongue to call, nor hands to wash; / And so let's leave her to her silent walks.
She has no tongue to call with and no hands to wash, so let's leave her to her silent walks.
An 'twere my cause, I should go hang myself.
If it were me, I would go and hang myself.
If thou hadst hands to help thee knit the cord.
If you had hands to help you tie the rope.

Who is this? My niece, that flies away so fast? / Cousin, a word; where is your husband? / If I do dream, would all my wealth would wake me! / If I do wake, some planet strike me down, / That I may slumber an eternal sleep! / Speak, gentle niece, what stern ungentle hands / Hath lopped and hewed and made thy body bare / Of her two branches, those sweet ornaments / Whose circling shadows kings have sought to sleep in, / And might not gain so great a happiness / As half thy love? Why dost not speak to me? / Alas, a crimson river of warm blood, / Like to a bubbling fountain stirred with wind, / Doth rise and fall between thy rosed lips, / Coming and going with thy honey breath. / But sure some Tereus hath deflowered thee, / And, lest thou shouldst detect him, cut thy tongue. / Ah, now thou turn'st away thy face for shame, / And notwithstanding all this loss of blood, / As from a conduit with three issuing spouts, / Yet do thy cheeks look red as Titan's face / Blushing to be encountered with a cloud. / Shall I speak for thee, shall I say 'tis so? / O, that I knew thy heart, and knew the beast, / That I might rail at him to ease my mind. / Sorrow concealed, like an oven stopped, / Doth burn the heart to cinders where it is. / Fair Philomela, why she but lost her tongue, / And in a tedious sampler sewed her mind; / But, lovely niece, that mean is cut from thee; / A craftier Tereus, cousin, hast thou met, / And he hath cut those pretty fingers off / That could have better sewed than Philomel. / O, had the monster seen those lily hands / Tremble like aspen leaves upon a lute, / And make the silken strings delight to kiss them, / He would not then have touched them for his life. / Or had he heard the heavenly harmony / Which that sweet tongue hath made, / He would have dropped his knife, and fell asleep, / As Cerberus at the Thracian poet's feet. / Come, let us go, and make thy father blind, / For such a sight will blind a father's eye. / One hour's storm will drown the fragrant meads; / What will whole months of tears thy father's eyes? / Do not draw back, for we will mourn with thee. / O, could our mourning ease thy misery!

Who is this? My niece, running away so fast? Niece, a word. Where is your husband? If I am dreaming, I would give all my wealth to wake up! If I am awake, may some planet strike me down so that I may sleep for ever! Speak, gentle niece: what harsh, cruel hands have lopped and hacked your body and stripped it of its two branches, those sweet ornaments whose embracing shade kings have longed to sleep in, and could not win so great a happiness as half your love? Why don't you speak to me? Alas, a crimson river of warm blood, like a bubbling fountain stirred by the wind, rises and falls between your rosy lips, coming and going with your sweet breath. Surely some Tereus has raped you, and cut out your tongue so that you could not expose him. Ah, now you turn your face away in shame. And in spite of all this loss of blood, pouring as if from a fountain with three spouts, your cheeks still look as red as the sun's face blushing when it meets a cloud. Shall I speak for you? Shall I say that is what happened? O, if only I knew your heart, and knew the beast, so that I could rage at him to ease my mind. Hidden sorrow, like a closed oven, burns the heart where it is to cinders. Fair Philomela only lost her tongue, and she stitched her story into a laborious piece of needlework. But, lovely niece, that way has been cut off from you. You have met a craftier Tereus, niece, and he has cut off those pretty fingers that could have sewn better than Philomela. O, if the monster had seen those lily-white hands tremble like aspen leaves on a lute and make the silk strings delight to kiss them, he would not have touched them to save his life. Or if he had heard the heavenly music that sweet tongue made, he would have dropped his knife and fallen asleep, as Cerberus did at the feet of Orpheus, the Thracian poet. Come, let us go and make your father blind, for such a sight will blind a father's eyes. One hour's storm will flood the sweet meadows: what will months of tears do to your father's eyes? Don't draw back, for we will mourn with you. O, if only our mourning could ease your misery!

Hear me, grave fathers; noble tribunes, stay! / For pity of mine age, whose youth was spent / In dangerous wars whilst you securely slept; / For all my blood in Rome's great quarrel shed, / For all the frosty nights that I have watched, / And for these bitter tears, which now you see / Filling the aged wrinkles in my cheeks, / Be pitiful to my condemned sons, / Whose souls are not corrupted as 'tis thought. / For two and twenty sons I never wept, / Because they died in honour's lofty bed.

Hear me, wise fathers! Noble tribunes, stop! Out of pity for my age, whose youth was spent in dangerous wars while you slept safely; for all the blood I have shed in Rome's great cause; for all the frosty nights I have kept watch; and for these bitter tears that you now see filling the old wrinkles in my cheeks: have mercy on my condemned sons, whose souls are not as corrupt as people think. I never wept for twenty-two sons, because they died in honour's noble bed.

For these, tribunes, in the dust I write / My heart's deep languor and my soul's sad tears. / Let my tears staunch the earth's dry appetite; / My sons' sweet blood will make it shame and blush. / O earth, I will befriend thee more with rain / That shall distil from these two ancient urns, / Than youthful April shall with all his showers. / In summer's drought I'll drop upon thee still; / In winter with warm tears I'll melt the snow, / And keep eternal spring-time on thy face, / So thou refuse to drink my dear sons' blood.

For these sons, tribunes, I write my heart's deep grief and my soul's sad tears in the dust. Let my tears satisfy the earth's dry hunger; my sons' sweet blood would make it blush with shame. O earth, I will water you more with rain dripping from these two old eyes than young April with all his showers. In summer's drought I'll keep dripping on you. In winter I'll melt the snow with warm tears and keep your face in eternal spring, if only you refuse to drink my dear sons' blood.
O reverend tribunes! O gentle aged men! / Unbind my sons, reverse the doom of death; / And let me say, that never wept before, / My tears are now prevailing orators.
O respected tribunes! O kind old men! Unbind my sons, overturn the sentence of death, and let me, who never wept before, say that my tears are now persuasive speakers.
O noble father, you lament in vain. / The tribunes hear you not, no man is by; / And you recount your sorrows to a stone.
O noble father, you are lamenting for nothing. The tribunes can't hear you. No one is here, and you are telling your sorrows to a stone.
Ah, Lucius, for thy brothers let me plead. / Grave tribunes, once more I entreat of you—
Ah, Lucius, let me plead for your brothers. Wise tribunes, once more I beg you—
My gracious lord, no tribune hears you speak.
My gracious lord, no tribune hears you speaking.

Why, 'tis no matter, man. If they did hear, / They would not mark me; if they did mark, / They would not pity me, yet plead I must, / And bootless unto them. / Therefore I tell my sorrows to the stones, / Who, though they cannot answer my distress, / Yet in some sort they are better than the tribunes, / For that they will not intercept my tale. / When I do weep, they humbly at my feet / Receive my tears, and seem to weep with me; / And were they but attired in grave weeds, / Rome could afford no tribunes like to these. / A stone is soft as wax, tribunes more hard than stones; / A stone is silent, and offendeth not, / And tribunes with their tongues doom men to death. / But wherefore stand'st thou with thy weapon drawn?

Why, it doesn't matter, man. If they did hear, they would not take notice of me. If they took notice, they would not pity me. Yet I must plead, uselessly, to them. So I tell my sorrows to the stones. Though they cannot answer my distress, they are in some ways better than the tribunes, because they will not interrupt my story. When I weep, they humbly take my tears at my feet and seem to weep with me. If only they were dressed in solemn robes, Rome could not provide tribunes as good as these. A stone is soft as wax; tribunes are harder than stones. A stone is silent and does no harm, and tribunes condemn men to death with their tongues. But why are you standing there with your sword drawn?
To rescue my two brothers from their death; / For which attempt the judges have pronounced / My everlasting doom of banishment.
To rescue my two brothers from death. For trying it, the judges have sentenced me to banishment for ever.

O happy man, they have befriended thee. / Why, foolish Lucius, dost thou not perceive / That Rome is but a wilderness of tigers? / Tigers must prey, and Rome affords no prey / But me and mine. How happy art thou then, / From these devourers to be banished! / But who comes with our brother Marcus here?

O lucky man, they have done you a favour. Why, foolish Lucius, can't you see that Rome is nothing but a wilderness of tigers? Tigers must hunt, and Rome has no prey for them but me and my family. How lucky you are, then, to be banished from these devourers! But who is coming here with our brother Marcus?
Titus, prepare thy aged eyes to weep; / Or if not so, thy noble heart to break. / I bring consuming sorrow to thine age.
Titus, get your old eyes ready to weep, or, if not, your noble heart to break. I am bringing a sorrow that will consume your old age.
Will it consume me? Let me see it then.
Will it consume me? Then let me see it.
Ay me, this object kills me!
Oh no, this sight is killing me!

Faint-hearted boy, arise, and look upon her. / Speak, Lavinia, what accursed hand / Hath made thee handless in thy father's sight? / What fool hath added water to the sea, / Or brought a faggot to bright-burning Troy? / My grief was at the height before thou cam'st, / And now like Nilus it disdaineth bounds. / Give me a sword, I'll chop off my hands too; / For they have fought for Rome, and all in vain; / And they have nursed this woe in feeding life; / In bootless prayer have they been held up, / And they have served me to effectless use. / Now all the service I require of them / Is that the one will help to cut the other. / 'Tis well, Lavinia, that thou hast no hands, / For hands to do Rome service is but vain.

Faint-hearted boy, get up and look at her. Speak, Lavinia: what cursed hand has made you handless in your father's sight? What fool has added water to the sea, or brought a bundle of sticks to Troy as it burned? My grief was at its height before you came, and now, like the Nile, it overflows its banks. Give me a sword. I'll chop off my hands too, for they have fought for Rome, all for nothing. They kept me alive to nurse this misery. They have been raised in useless prayer, and they have served me to no purpose. Now the only service I want from them is for one to help cut off the other. It is just as well, Lavinia, that you have no hands, for hands that serve Rome are useless.
Speak, gentle sister, who hath martyred thee?
Speak, gentle sister, who has tortured you?

O, that delightful engine of her thoughts, / That blabbed them with such pleasing eloquence, / Is torn from forth that pretty hollow cage, / Where, like a sweet melodious bird, it sung / Sweet varied notes, enchanting every ear.

O, that delightful instrument of her thoughts, which told them with such pleasing eloquence, has been torn out of that pretty hollow cage where it sang sweet, varied notes like a sweet singing bird, enchanting every ear.
O, say thou for her, who hath done this deed?
O, you say it for her: who has done this?
O, thus I found her straying in the park, / Seeking to hide herself, as doth the deer / That hath received some unrecuring wound.
O, I found her like this, wandering in the park, trying to hide herself, like a deer that has been given an incurable wound.

It was my dear, and he that wounded her / Hath hurt me more than had he killed me dead. / For now I stand as one upon a rock, / Environed with a wilderness of sea, / Who marks the waxing tide grow wave by wave, / Expecting ever when some envious surge / Will in his brinish bowels swallow him. / This way to death my wretched sons are gone; / Here stands my other son, a banished man, / And here my brother, weeping at my woes. / But that which gives my soul the greatest spurn / Is dear Lavinia, dearer than my soul. / Had I but seen thy picture in this plight / It would have madded me. What shall I do / Now I behold thy lively body so? / Thou hast no hands to wipe away thy tears, / Nor tongue to tell me who hath martyred thee. / Thy husband he is dead, and for his death / Thy brothers are condemned, and dead by this. / Look, Marcus! Ah, son Lucius, look on her! / When I did name her brothers, then fresh tears / Stood on her cheeks, as doth the honey-dew / Upon a gathered lily almost withered.

She was my dear, and whoever wounded her has hurt me more than if he had killed me. For now I am like a man standing on a rock, surrounded by a wilderness of sea, who watches the rising tide grow wave by wave, always waiting for some spiteful wave to swallow him in its salty belly. This way my wretched sons have gone to their deaths. Here stands my other son, a banished man, and here my brother, weeping at my sorrows. But what wounds my soul most is dear Lavinia, dearer than my soul. If I had only seen a picture of you in this state, it would have driven me mad. What shall I do, now that I see your living body like this? You have no hands to wipe away your tears, no tongue to tell me who has tortured you. Your husband is dead, and for his death your brothers are condemned, and dead by now. Look, Marcus! Ah, son Lucius, look at her! When I mentioned her brothers, fresh tears stood on her cheeks, like honeydew on a picked lily that is almost withered.
Perchance she weeps because they killed her husband; / Perchance because she knows them innocent.
Perhaps she is weeping because they killed her husband; perhaps because she knows they are innocent.

If they did kill thy husband, then be joyful, / Because the law hath ta'en revenge on them. / No, no, they would not do so foul a deed; / Witness the sorrow that their sister makes. / Gentle Lavinia, let me kiss thy lips, / Or make some sign how I may do thee ease. / Shall thy good uncle, and thy brother Lucius, / And thou, and I, sit round about some fountain, / Looking all downwards to behold our cheeks / How they are stained, like meadows yet not dry, / With miry slime left on them by a flood? / And in the fountain shall we gaze so long / Till the fresh taste be taken from that clearness, / And made a brine-pit with our bitter tears? / Or shall we cut away our hands like thine? / Or shall we bite our tongues, and in dumb shows / Pass the remainder of our hateful days? / What shall we do? Let us that have our tongues / Plot some device of further misery, / To make us wondered at in time to come.

If they did kill your husband, then be glad, because the law has taken revenge on them. No, no, they would never do such a foul deed: look at how their sister grieves. Gentle Lavinia, let me kiss your lips, or make some sign of how I can comfort you. Shall your good uncle and your brother Lucius and you and I sit round some fountain, all looking down to see how our cheeks are stained, like meadows not yet dry, with muddy slime left by a flood? And shall we stare into the fountain so long that its fresh taste is spoiled and our bitter tears turn it into a pool of brine? Or shall we cut off our hands like yours? Or bite off our tongues, and spend the rest of our hateful days in dumb show? What shall we do? Let those of us who still have tongues plan some further misery, to make people marvel at us in times to come.
Sweet father, cease your tears; for at your grief / See how my wretched sister sobs and weeps.
Sweet father, stop crying, for look how my poor sister sobs and weeps at your grief.
Patience, dear niece. Good Titus, dry thine eyes.
Be patient, dear niece. Good Titus, dry your eyes.
Ah, Marcus, Marcus! Brother, well I wot / Thy napkin cannot drink a tear of mine, / For thou, poor man, hast drowned it with thine own.
Ah, Marcus, Marcus! Brother, I know very well that your handkerchief cannot soak up a single tear of mine, because you, poor man, have drowned it with your own.
Ah, my Lavinia, I will wipe thy cheeks.
Ah, my Lavinia, I will wipe your cheeks.

Mark, Marcus, mark! I understand her signs. / Had she a tongue to speak, now would she say / That to her brother which I said to thee. / His napkin, with his true tears all bewet, / Can do no service on her sorrowful cheeks. / O, what a sympathy of woe is this, / As far from help as limbo is from bliss.

Look, Marcus, look! I understand her signs. If she had a tongue to speak, she would say to her brother now what I just said to you: his handkerchief, soaked with his own true tears, is no use on her sorrowful cheeks. O, what a sharing of grief this is, as far from help as limbo is from heaven.

Titus Andronicus, my lord the emperor / Sends thee this word, that, if thou love thy sons, / Let Marcus, Lucius, or thyself, old Titus, / Or any one of you, chop off your hand / And send it to the king; he for the same / Will send thee hither both thy sons alive, / And that shall be the ransom for their fault.

Titus Andronicus, my lord the emperor sends you this message: if you love your sons, let Marcus, Lucius or yourself, old Titus, or any one of you, chop off your hand and send it to the king. In return he will send both your sons back here alive, and that will be the ransom for their crime.

O gracious emperor! O gentle Aaron! / Did ever raven sing so like a lark / That gives sweet tidings of the sun's uprise? / With all my heart I'll send the emperor my hand. / Good Aaron, wilt thou help to chop it off?
O gracious emperor! O kind Aaron! Did a raven ever sing so like a lark, bringing the sweet news of sunrise? With all my heart I'll send the emperor my hand. Good Aaron, will you help to chop it off?

Stay, father, for that noble hand of thine, / That hath thrown down so many enemies, / Shall not be sent. My hand will serve the turn. / My youth can better spare my blood than you; / And therefore mine shall save my brothers' lives.

Wait, father, for that noble hand of yours, which has struck down so many enemies, shall not be sent. My hand will do the job. Being young, I can spare my blood better than you, and so mine shall save my brothers' lives.

Which of your hands hath not defended Rome, / And reared aloft the bloody battle-axe, / Writing destruction on the enemy's castle? / O, none of both but are of high desert. / My hand hath been but idle; let it serve / To ransom my two nephews from their death; / Then have I kept it to a worthy end.

Which of your hands has not defended Rome and raised the bloody battle-axe high, writing destruction on the enemy's castle? O, both of you have hands that have earned great honour. My hand has done nothing. Let it serve to ransom my two nephews from death; then I will have kept it for a worthy purpose.
Nay, come, agree whose hand shall go along, / For fear they die before their pardon come.
No, come, agree whose hand is going, in case they die before their pardon comes.
By heaven, it shall not go!
Sirs, strive no more. Such withered herbs as these / Are meet for plucking up, and therefore mine.
Sirs, stop arguing. Withered weeds like these are the right ones to pull up, and so it must be mine.
Sweet father, if I shall be thought thy son, / Let me redeem my brothers both from death.
Sweet father, if I am to be thought your son, let me save both my brothers from death.
And for our father's sake and mother's care, / Now let me show a brother's love to thee.
And for the sake of our father and our mother's care, let me show you a brother's love now.
Agree between you; I will spare my hand.
Settle it between you. I will keep my hand.
Then I'll go fetch an axe.
Then I'll go and fetch an axe.
But I will use the axe.
But I will be the one to use it.
Come hither, Aaron; I'll deceive them both. / Lend me thy hand, and I will give thee mine.
Come here, Aaron. I'll trick them both. Lend me your hand, and I will give you mine.
[Aside] If that be called deceit, I will be honest, / And never whilst I live deceive men so. / But I'll deceive you in another sort, / And that you'll say ere half an hour pass.
(Aside) If that is called deceit, I will be honest, and never deceive men like that as long as I live. But I'll deceive you in another way, as you'll admit within half an hour.

Now stay your strife. What shall be is dispatched. / Good Aaron, give his majesty my hand. / Tell him it was a hand that warded him / From thousand dangers, bid him bury it; / More hath it merited, that let it have. / As for my sons, say I account of them / As jewels purchased at an easy price; / And yet dear too, because I bought mine own.

Now stop your quarrel. What had to be done is done. Good Aaron, give his majesty my hand. Tell him it was a hand that protected him from a thousand dangers, and ask him to bury it. It has deserved more; let it have that much. As for my sons, tell him I count them as jewels bought cheaply, and yet dearly too, because I have only bought back what was mine.

I go, Andronicus; and for thy hand / Look by and by to have thy sons with thee. / [Aside] Their heads, I mean. O, how this villainy / Doth fat me with the very thoughts of it! / Let fools do good, and fair men call for grace, / Aaron will have his soul black like his face.

I'm going, Andronicus, and in return for your hand expect to have your sons with you soon. (Aside) Their heads, I mean. O, how this villainy fattens me just to think of it! Let fools do good, and fair-skinned men pray for grace: Aaron will have his soul as black as his face.

O, here I lift this one hand up to heaven, / And bow this feeble ruin to the earth. / If any power pities wretched tears, / To that I call! [To Lavinia] What, wouldst thou kneel with me? / Do, then, dear heart; for heaven shall hear our prayers, / Or with our sighs we'll breathe the welkin dim, / And stain the sun with fog, as sometime clouds / When they do hug him in their melting bosoms.

O, here I lift this one hand up to heaven, and bow this feeble ruin of a body to the ground. If any power pities wretched tears, I call on it! (To Lavinia) What, would you kneel with me? Do, then, dear heart, for heaven shall hear our prayers, or we'll darken the sky with our sighs and smear the sun with fog, as clouds sometimes do when they hug him in their melting arms.
O brother, speak with possibility, / And do not break into these deep extremes.
O brother, talk of what is possible, and do not burst into these extremes.
Is not my sorrow deep, having no bottom? / Then be my passions bottomless with them.
Isn't my sorrow deep, when it has no bottom? Then let my passions be as bottomless.
But yet let reason govern thy lament.
But still, let reason rule your grief.

If there were reason for these miseries, / Then into limits could I bind my woes. / When heaven doth weep, doth not the earth o'erflow? / If the winds rage, doth not the sea wax mad, / Threatening the welkin with his big-swol'n face? / And wilt thou have a reason for this coil? / I am the sea. Hark how her sighs doth flow! / She is the weeping welkin, I the earth. / Then must my sea be moved with her sighs; / Then must my earth with her continual tears / Become a deluge, overflowed and drowned; / For why my bowels cannot hide her woes, / But like a drunkard must I vomit them. / Then give me leave, for losers will have leave / To ease their stomachs with their bitter tongues.

If there were any reason for these miseries, then I could keep my sorrows within limits. When heaven weeps, doesn't the earth flood? If the winds rage, doesn't the sea go mad, threatening the sky with its great swollen face? And do you want a reason for this turmoil? I am the sea. Listen to how her sighs blow! She is the weeping sky, and I am the earth. So my sea must be stirred by her sighs. So my earth must be flooded and drowned by her endless tears. For my insides cannot hold her sorrows, but must vomit them up like a drunkard. So give me licence, for losers are allowed to ease their stomachs with bitter words.

Worthy Andronicus, ill art thou repaid / For that good hand thou sent'st the emperor. / Here are the heads of thy two noble sons, / And here's thy hand, in scorn to thee sent back. / Thy grief their sports, thy resolution mocked; / That woe is me to think upon thy woes, / More than remembrance of my father's death.

Worthy Andronicus, you are badly repaid for the good hand you sent the emperor. Here are the heads of your two noble sons, and here is your hand, sent back to you in scorn. Your grief is their entertainment, and your courage is mocked. It grieves me more to think of your sorrows than to remember my own father's death.

Now let hot Etna cool in Sicily, / And be my heart an ever-burning hell! / These miseries are more than may be borne. / To weep with them that weep doth ease some deal, / But sorrow flouted at is double death.

Now let hot Etna in Sicily grow cold, and let my heart be a hell that burns for ever! These miseries are more than anyone can bear. Weeping with those who weep gives some relief, but sorrow that is mocked is a double death.
Ah, that this sight should make so deep a wound, / And yet detested life not shrink thereat! / That ever death should let life bear his name, / Where life hath no more interest but to breathe!
Ah, that this sight should make so deep a wound, and yet hateful life does not shrink away from it! That death should ever let life go by his name, when life has no part left in it except breathing!
Alas, poor heart, that kiss is comfortless / As frozen water to a starved snake.
Alas, poor heart, that kiss is as little comfort as frozen water to a starving snake.
When will this fearful slumber have an end?
When will this terrible nightmare end?

Now farewell, flattery; die, Andronicus; / Thou dost not slumber. See thy two sons' heads, / Thy warlike hand, thy mangled daughter here; / Thy other banished son with this dear sight / Struck pale and bloodless; and thy brother, I, / Even like a stony image, cold and numb. / Ah, now no more will I control thy griefs. / Rent off thy silver hair, thy other hand / Gnawing with thy teeth; and be this dismal sight / The closing up of our most wretched eyes. / Now is a time to storm; why art thou still?

Now goodbye to comforting lies. Die, Andronicus: you are not dreaming. Look at your two sons' heads, your warrior's hand, your mutilated daughter here, your other son, banished, struck pale and bloodless by this dreadful sight, and your brother, me, cold and numb like a statue. Ah, I won't try to restrain your grief any more. Tear out your silver hair, gnaw your other hand with your teeth, and let this dreadful sight be the last thing our wretched eyes see before they close. Now is the time to rage. Why are you so quiet?
Why dost thou laugh? It fits not with this hour.
Why are you laughing? It doesn't suit this moment.

Why, I have not another tear to shed. / Besides, this sorrow is an enemy, / And would usurp upon my watery eyes, / And make them blind with tributary tears. / Then which way shall I find Revenge's cave? / For these two heads do seem to speak to me, / And threat me I shall never come to bliss / Till all these mischiefs be returned again / Even in their throats that have committed them. / Come, let me see what task I have to do. / You heavy people, circle me about, / That I may turn me to each one of you, / And swear unto my soul to right your wrongs. / The vow is made. Come, brother, take a head; / And in this hand the other will I bear. / And, Lavinia, thou shalt be employed in these arms. / Bear thou my hand, sweet wench, between thy teeth. / As for thee, boy, go, get thee from my sight; / Thou art an exile, and thou must not stay. / Hie to the Goths, and raise an army there. / And if you love me, as I think you do, / Let's kiss and part, for we have much to do.

Why, I haven't another tear to shed. Besides, this sorrow is an enemy that wants to take over my watering eyes and blind them with the tears they pay it. Then how shall I find the cave of Revenge? For these two heads seem to speak to me, and threaten that I shall never reach heaven until all these crimes are thrust back down the throats of those who committed them. Come, let me see what work I have to do. You sorrowing people, stand in a circle round me, so that I can turn to each of you and swear on my soul to right your wrongs. The vow is made. Come, brother, take a head, and I will carry the other in this hand. And, Lavinia, you shall have a job too. Carry my hand between your teeth, sweet girl. As for you, boy, go, get out of my sight. You are an exile, and you must not stay. Hurry to the Goths and raise an army there. And if you love me, as I think you do, let's kiss and part, for we have much to do.

Farewell, Andronicus, my noble father, / The woefull'st man that ever lived in Rome. / Farewell, proud Rome, till Lucius come again; / He loves his pledges dearer than his life. / Farewell, Lavinia, my noble sister; / O, would thou wert as thou tofore hast been! / But now nor Lucius nor Lavinia lives / But in oblivion and hateful griefs. / If Lucius live, he will requite your wrongs, / And make proud Saturnine and his empress / Beg at the gates, like Tarquin and his queen. / Now will I to the Goths, and raise a power / To be revenged on Rome and Saturnine.

Farewell, Andronicus, my noble father, the most miserable man who ever lived in Rome. Farewell, proud Rome, until Lucius comes again: he leaves behind those he loves more than his life. Farewell, Lavinia, my noble sister. O, if only you were as you used to be! But now neither Lucius nor Lavinia lives, except in being forgotten and in hateful grief. If Lucius lives, he will repay your wrongs, and make proud Saturnine and his empress beg at the gates, like Tarquin and his queen. Now I'll go to the Goths and raise an army to take revenge on Rome and Saturnine.

So so; now sit; and look you eat no more / Than will preserve just so much strength in us / As will revenge these bitter woes of ours. / Marcus, unknit that sorrow-wreathen knot. / Thy niece and I, poor creatures, want our hands, / And cannot passionate our tenfold grief / With folded arms. This poor right hand of mine / Is left to tyrannize upon my breast; / Who when my heart, all mad with misery, / Beats in this hollow prison of my flesh, / Then thus I thump it down. / Thou map of woe, that thus dost talk in signs, / When thy poor heart beats with outrageous beating, / Thou canst not strike it thus to make it still. / Wound it with sighing, girl, kill it with groans; / Or get some little knife between thy teeth, / And just against thy heart make thou a hole, / That all the tears that thy poor eyes let fall / May run into that sink, and, soaking in, / Drown the lamenting fool in sea-salt tears.

There, there. Now sit down, and make sure you eat no more than will keep just enough strength in us to avenge these bitter sorrows of ours. Marcus, undo that sad knot of folded arms. Your niece and I, poor creatures, have no hands, and cannot show our tenfold grief by folding our arms. This poor right hand of mine is left to beat cruelly on my breast, and when my heart, mad with misery, pounds in this hollow prison of my flesh, I thump it down like this. (To Lavinia) You picture of grief, who talk in signs: when your poor heart beats wildly, you cannot strike it like this to quieten it. Wound it with sighs, girl, kill it with groans. Or take some little knife between your teeth and make a hole just over your heart, so that all the tears your poor eyes shed may run into that drain and soak in, and drown the grieving fool in salt tears.
Fie, brother, fie! Teach her not thus to lay / Such violent hands upon her tender life.
For shame, brother! Don't teach her to lay such violent hands on her own young life.

How now! Has sorrow made thee dote already? / Why, Marcus, no man should be mad but I. / What violent hands can she lay on her life? / Ah, wherefore dost thou urge the name of hands, / To bid Æneas tell the tale twice o'er / How Troy was burnt and he made miserable? / O, handle not the theme, to talk of hands, / Lest we remember still that we have none. / Fie, fie, how frantically I square my talk, / As if we should forget we had no hands, / If Marcus did not name the word of hands! / Come, let's fall to; and, gentle girl, eat this. / Here is no drink! Hark, Marcus, what she says; / I can interpret all her martyred signs. / She says she drinks no other drink but tears, / Brewed with her sorrow, meshed upon her cheeks. / Speechless complainer, I will learn thy thought; / In thy dumb action will I be as perfect / As begging hermits in their holy prayers. / Thou shalt not sigh, nor hold thy stumps to heaven, / Nor wink, nor nod, nor kneel, nor make a sign, / But I of these will wrest an alphabet, / And by still practice learn to know thy meaning.

What's this! Has sorrow made you senile already? Why, Marcus, no one should be mad but me. What violent hands can she lay on her life? Ah, why do you keep on about hands? It's like asking Aeneas to tell the story twice of how Troy was burnt and he was made miserable. O, don't touch the subject of hands, in case we keep remembering that we have none. Ugh, how madly I am shaping my words, as if we would forget we had no hands if Marcus did not say the word! Come, let's start eating. And, gentle girl, eat this. There's nothing to drink! Listen, Marcus, to what she says. I can interpret all her tortured signs. She says she drinks no drink but tears, brewed from her sorrow and mashed on her cheeks. Speechless complainer, I will learn your thoughts. I will be as perfect in your silent gestures as begging hermits are in their holy prayers. You shall not sigh, or hold your stumps up to heaven, or wink, nod, kneel or make a sign, but I will wring an alphabet out of it and by constant practice learn to know what you mean.
Good grandsire, leave these bitter deep laments. / Make my aunt merry with some pleasing tale.
Good grandfather, stop these bitter, deep laments. Cheer my aunt up with some nice story.
Alas, the tender boy, in passion moved, / Doth weep to see his grandsire's heaviness.
Alas, the tender boy is so moved that he weeps to see his grandfather's sadness.
Peace, tender sapling; thou art made of tears, / And tears will quickly melt thy life away.
Quiet, tender young tree. You are made of tears, and tears will soon melt your life away.
What dost thou strike at, Marcus, with thy knife?
What are you striking at with your knife, Marcus?
At that that I have killed, my lord, a fly.
At something I have killed, my lord: a fly.

Out on thee, murderer! Thou kill'st my heart; / Mine eyes are cloyed with view of tyranny; / A deed of death done on the innocent / Becomes not Titus' brother. Get thee gone; / I see thou art not for my company.

Shame on you, murderer! You are killing my heart. My eyes have seen too much cruelty. A deed of death done to the innocent does not suit Titus's brother. Go away. I can see you're not fit for my company.
Alas, my lord, I have but killed a fly.
Alas, my lord, I have only killed a fly.

"But"? How if that fly had a father and mother? / How would he hang his slender gilded wings / And buzz lamenting doings in the air! / Poor harmless fly, / That with his pretty buzzing melody, / Came here to make us merry, and thou hast killed him.

'Only'? What if that fly had a father and mother? How he would droop his slender golden wings and buzz his grief in the air! Poor harmless fly, who came here with his pretty buzzing tune to cheer us up, and you have killed him.
Pardon me, sir; 'twas a black ill-favoured fly, / Like to the empress' Moor; therefore I killed him.
Forgive me, sir. It was a black, ugly fly, like the empress's Moor. That's why I killed him.

O, O, O! / Then pardon me for reprehending thee, / For thou hast done a charitable deed. / Give me thy knife, I will insult on him, / Flattering myself as if it were the Moor / Come hither purposely to poison me. / There's for thyself, and that's for Tamora. / Ah, sirrah! / Yet, I think, we are not brought so low / But that between us we can kill a fly / That comes in likeness of a coal-black Moor.

O, O, O! Then forgive me for scolding you, for you have done a good deed. Give me your knife. I will gloat over him, pretending to myself that it is the Moor, come here on purpose to poison me. There's one for you, and that's for Tamora. Ah, you rascal! And yet I think we are not brought so low that between us we can't kill a fly that comes looking like a coal-black Moor.
Alas, poor man, grief has so wrought on him, / He takes false shadows for true substances.
Alas, poor man, grief has worked on him so much that he mistakes false shadows for real things.

Come, take away. Lavinia, go with me. / I'll to thy closet, and go read with thee / Sad stories chanced in the times of old. / Come, boy, and go with me. Thy sight is young, / And thou shalt read when mine begin to dazzle.

Come, clear the table. Lavinia, come with me. I'll go to your room and read with you sad stories of things that happened long ago. Come, boy, come with me. Your eyes are young, and you shall read when mine start to blur.
Help, grandsire, help! My aunt Lavinia / Follows me everywhere, I know not why. / Good uncle Marcus, see how swift she comes! / Alas, sweet aunt, I know not what you mean.
Help, grandfather, help! My aunt Lavinia follows me everywhere, I don't know why. Good uncle Marcus, see how fast she's coming! Oh, sweet aunt, I don't know what you mean.
Stand by me, Lucius. Do not fear thine aunt.
Stand by me, Lucius. Don't be afraid of your aunt.
She loves thee, boy, too well to do thee harm.
She loves you too well to hurt you, boy.
Ay, when my father was in Rome she did.
Yes, when my father was in Rome, she did.
What means my niece Lavinia by these signs?
What does my niece Lavinia mean by these signs?

Fear her not, Lucius. Somewhat doth she mean. / See, Lucius, see how much she makes of thee. / Somewhither would she have thee go with her. / Ah, boy, Cornelia never with more care / Read to her sons than she hath read to thee / Sweet poetry and Tully's Orator.

Don't be afraid of her, Lucius. She means something. See, Lucius, how fond she is of you. She wants you to go somewhere with her. Ah, boy, Cornelia never read to her sons with more care than Lavinia has read sweet poetry and Cicero's 'Orator' to you.
Canst thou not guess wherefore she plies thee thus?
Can't you guess why she keeps after you like this?

My lord, I know not, I, nor can I guess, / Unless some fit or frenzy do possess her; / For I have heard my grandsire say full oft, / Extremity of griefs would make men mad; / And I have read that Hecuba of Troy / Ran mad for sorrow. That made me to fear, / Although, my lord, I know my noble aunt / Loves me as dear as e'er my mother did, / And would not, but in fury, fright my youth; / Which made me down to throw my books, and fly, / Causeless, perhaps. But pardon me, sweet aunt. / And, madam, if my uncle Marcus go, / I will most willingly attend your ladyship.

My lord, I don't know, and I can't guess, unless some fit or frenzy has taken hold of her. For I have often heard my grandfather say that extreme grief can drive people mad, and I have read that Hecuba of Troy went mad with sorrow. That made me afraid. Though, my lord, I know my noble aunt loves me as dearly as my mother ever did, and would not frighten me, being young, unless she were mad. That made me throw down my books and run, without cause, perhaps. Forgive me, sweet aunt. And, madam, if my uncle Marcus will come, I will gladly go with your ladyship.

How now, Lavinia? Marcus, what means this? / Some book there is that she desires to see. / Which is it, girl, of these? Open them, boy. / But thou art deeper read and better skilled. / Come and take choice of all my library, / And so beguile thy sorrow, till the heavens / Reveal the damned contriver of this deed. / Why lifts she up her arms in sequence thus?

What is it, Lavinia? Marcus, what does this mean? There is some book here she wants to see. Which of these is it, girl? Open them, boy. (To Lavinia) But you are more widely read and more skilled. Come and choose from my whole library, and so distract yourself from your sorrow until heaven reveals the damned plotter of this deed. Why does she lift up her arms one after the other like that?
I think she means that there were more than one / Confederate in the fact. Ay, more there was, / Or else to heaven she heaves them for revenge.
I think she means that more than one person was involved in the crime. Yes, there was more than one. Or else she is raising them to heaven for revenge.
Lucius, what book is that she tosseth so?
Lucius, what book is that she is tossing about?
Grandsire, 'tis Ovid's Metamorphosis. / My mother gave it me.
Grandfather, it's Ovid's Metamorphoses. My mother gave it to me.
For love of her that's gone, / Perhaps, she culled it from among the rest.
Perhaps she picked it out from the rest out of love for her who is gone.

Soft! So busily she turns the leaves! / Help her! What would she find? Lavinia, shall I read? / This is the tragic tale of Philomel, / And treats of Tereus' treason and his rape; / And rape, I fear, was root of thy annoy.

Wait! How busily she turns the pages! Help her! What does she want to find? Lavinia, shall I read? This is the tragic tale of Philomela, and it tells of Tereus's treachery and his rape. And rape, I fear, was the root of your suffering.
See, brother, see! Note how she quotes the leaves.
See, brother, see! Look how she points to the pages.

Lavinia, wert thou thus surprised, sweet girl, / Ravished and wronged, as Philomela was, / Forced in the ruthless, vast, and gloomy woods? / See, see! / Ay, such a place there is where we did hunt,— / O, had we never, never hunted there!— / Patterned by that the poet here describes, / By nature made for murders and for rapes.

Lavinia, were you caught like this, sweet girl, raped and wronged as Philomela was, taken by force in the pitiless, vast and gloomy woods? Look, look! Yes, there is such a place where we went hunting (O, if only we had never, never hunted there!), just like the one the poet describes here, made by nature for murders and rapes.
O, why should nature build so foul a den, / Unless the gods delight in tragedies?
O, why would nature build such a foul den, unless the gods enjoy tragedies?
Give signs, sweet girl, for here are none but friends, / What Roman lord it was durst do the deed. / Or slunk not Saturnine, as Tarquin erst, / That left the camp to sin in Lucrece' bed?

Sweet girl, make signs to tell us, for there are only friends here, which Roman lord it was who dared to do this. Or did Saturnine creep off, as Tarquin once did when he left the camp to sin in Lucrece's bed?

Sit down, sweet niece. Brother, sit down by me. / Apollo, Pallas, Jove, or Mercury, / Inspire me, that I may this treason find! / My lord, look here. Look here, Lavinia. / This sandy plot is plain; guide, if thou canst, / This after me. I have writ my name

Sit down, sweet niece. Brother, sit down beside me. Apollo, Pallas, Jove or Mercury, inspire me so that I can uncover this treachery! My lord, look here. Look here, Lavinia. This patch of sand is smooth. Copy this after me, if you can. I have written my name

Without the help of any hand at all. / Cursed be that heart that forced us to this shift! / Write thou, good niece, and here display at last / What God will have discovered for revenge. / Heaven guide thy pen to print thy sorrows plain, / That we may know the traitors and the truth!

without the help of any hand at all. Cursed be the heart that forced us to this trick! Write, good niece, and show here at last what God wants revealed for revenge. May heaven guide your pen to write your sorrows plainly, so that we may know the traitors and the truth!
O, do ye read, my lord, what she hath writ?
O, do you read, my lord, what she has written?
What, what! The lustful sons of Tamora / Performers of this heinous bloody deed?
What, what! Tamora's lustful sons did this terrible, bloody deed?
Magni Dominator poli, / Tam lentus audis scelera, tam lentus vides?
Great ruler of the heavens, are you so slow to hear crimes, so slow to see them?

O, calm thee, gentle lord, although I know / There is enough written upon this earth / To stir a mutiny in the mildest thoughts / And arm the minds of infants to exclaims. / My lord, kneel down with me; Lavinia, kneel; / And kneel, sweet boy, the Roman Hector's hope; / And swear with me, as, with the woeful fere / And father of that chaste dishonoured dame, / Lord Junius Brutus sware for Lucrece' rape, / That we will prosecute, by good advice / Mortal revenge upon these traitorous Goths, / And see their blood, or die with this reproach.

O, calm yourself, gentle lord, though I know there is enough written on this ground to start a rebellion in the mildest mind and arm the minds of babies with outcries. My lord, kneel down with me. Lavinia, kneel. And kneel, sweet boy, the hope of Rome's Hector. And swear with me, as Lord Junius Brutus swore with the grieving husband and the father of that chaste, dishonoured lady after the rape of Lucrece, that with careful planning we will pursue deadly revenge on these treacherous Goths, and see their blood, or die with this disgrace.

'Tis sure enough, an you knew how. / But if you hunt these bear-whelps, then beware; / The dam will wake, and if she wind you once. / She's with the lion deeply still in league, / And lulls him whilst she playeth on her back, / And when he sleeps will she do what she list. / You are a young huntsman, Marcus; let alone; / And come, I will go get a leaf of brass, / And with a gad of steel will write these words, / And lay it by. The angry northern wind / Will blow these sands like Sibyl's leaves abroad, / And where's our lesson, then? Boy, what say you?

That's sure enough, if you knew how. But if you hunt these bear cubs, be careful: the mother will wake if she once gets your scent. She is still in close league with the lion, and lulls him while she lies on her back, and when he sleeps she does whatever she likes. You are a young huntsman, Marcus. Leave it alone. And come, I will get a sheet of brass and carve these words into it with a steel point, and keep it safe. The angry north wind will scatter these sands like the Sibyl's leaves, and where's our lesson then? Boy, what do you say?
I say, my lord, that if I were a man, / Their mother's bedchamber should not be safe / For these base bondmen to the yoke of Rome.
I say, my lord, that if I were a man, their mother's bedroom would not be safe for these low slaves of the Roman yoke.
Ay, that's my boy! Thy father hath full oft / For his ungrateful country done the like.
Yes, that's my boy! Your father has often done the same for his ungrateful country.
And, uncle, so will I, an if I live.
And, uncle, so will I, if I live.

Come, go with me into mine armoury. / Lucius, I'll fit thee; and withal, my boy, / Shall carry from me to the empress' sons / Presents that I intend to send them both. / Come, come; thou'lt do my message, wilt thou not?
Come with me into my armoury. Lucius, I'll equip you, and you shall also carry presents from me to the empress's sons, which I mean to send them both. Come, come, you'll carry my message, won't you?
Ay, with my dagger in their bosoms, grandsire.
Yes, with my dagger in their hearts, grandfather.
No, boy, not so. I'll teach thee another course. / Lavinia, come. Marcus, look to my house. / Lucius and I'll go brave it at the court; / Ay, marry, will we, sir; and we'll be waited on.
No, boy, not that. I'll teach you another way. Lavinia, come. Marcus, look after my house. Lucius and I will go and make a show at court. Yes, indeed we will, sir, and we'll be attended to.

O heavens, can you hear a good man groan / And not relent, or not compassion him? / Marcus, attend him in his ecstasy, / That hath more scars of sorrow in his heart / Than foemen's marks upon his battered shield, / But yet so just that he will not revenge. / Revenge ye heavens for old Andronicus!

O heavens, can you hear a good man groan and not soften or pity him? Marcus, look after him in his madness. He has more scars of sorrow in his heart than enemy marks on his battered shield, and yet he is so just that he will not take revenge. Heavens, take revenge for old Andronicus!
Demetrius, here's the son of Lucius; / He hath some message to deliver us.
Demetrius, here's Lucius's son. He has some message to give us.
Ay, some mad message from his mad grandfather.
Yes, some mad message from his mad grandfather.
My lords, with all the humbleness I may, / I greet your honours from Andronicus; / [Aside] And pray the Roman gods confound you both.
My lords, with all the humility I can, I greet your honours from Andronicus. (Aside) And I pray the Roman gods destroy you both.
Gramercy, lovely Lucius. What's the news?
Thank you, lovely Lucius. What's the news?

[Aside] That you are both deciphered, that's the news, / For villains marked with rape. [Aloud] May it please you, / My grandsire, well advised, hath sent by me / The goodliest weapons of his armoury / To gratify your honourable youth, / The hope of Rome; for so he bid me say; / And so I do, and with his gifts present / Your lordships, that, whenever you have need, / You may be armed and appointed well. / And so I leave you both, [Aside] like bloody villains.

(Aside) That you have both been found out as villains branded with rape: that's the news. (Aloud) If you please, my grandfather, after careful thought, has sent by me the finest weapons in his armoury as a present for your honourable youth, the hope of Rome. That's what he told me to say, and so I do, and I present your lordships with his gifts, so that whenever you need to, you may be well armed and equipped. And so I leave you both, (Aside) like bloody villains.
What's here? A scroll; and written round about? / Let's see: / [Reads] Integer vitae, scelerisque purus, / Non eget Mauri iaculis, nec arcu.
What's this? A scroll, with writing all round it? Let's see. (Reads) 'The man of upright life, free from crime, needs no Moorish javelins or bow.'
O, 'tis a verse in Horace; I know it well. / I read it in the grammar long ago.
O, it's a verse from Horace. I know it well. I read it in my Latin grammar long ago.

Ay, just; a verse in Horace; right, you have it. / [Aside] Now, what a thing it is to be an ass! / Here's no sound jest! The old man hath found their guilt, / And sends them weapons wrapped about with lines, / That wound, beyond their feeling, to the quick. / But were our witty empress well afoot, / She would applaud Andronicus' conceit. / But let her rest in her unrest awhile.— / And now, young lords, was't not a happy star / Led us to Rome, strangers, and more than so, / Captives, to be advanced to this height? / It did me good before the palace gate / To brave the tribune in his brother's hearing.

Yes, exactly, a verse from Horace. Right, you've got it. (Aside) Now, what a thing it is to be an ass! This is no joke! The old man has found out their guilt, and sends them weapons wrapped in verses that cut them to the quick without their feeling it. If our clever empress were up and about, she would applaud Andronicus's idea. But let her rest in her restlessness for a while. (To them) And now, young lords, wasn't it a lucky star that led us to Rome as strangers, and worse, as captives, to be raised to this height? It did me good to defy the tribune in front of the palace gate, where his brother could hear.
But me more good to see so great a lord / Basely insinuate and send us gifts.
But it did me more good to see so great a lord crawl humbly and send us gifts.
Had he not reason, Lord Demetrius? / Did you not use his daughter very friendly?
Hadn't he reason to, Lord Demetrius? Didn't you treat his daughter in a very friendly way?
I would we had a thousand Roman dames / At such a bay, by turn to serve our lust.
I wish we had a thousand Roman ladies cornered like that, to take turns serving our lust.
A charitable wish, and full of love.
A charitable wish, and full of love.
Here lacks but your mother for to say amen.
All we need now is your mother to say amen.
And that would she for twenty thousand more.
And she would, for twenty thousand more.
Come, let us go and pray to all the gods / For our beloved mother in her pains.
Come, let us go and pray to all the gods for our beloved mother in her labour pains.
[Aside] Pray to the devils; the gods have given us over.
(Aside) Pray to the devils: the gods have given up on us.
Why do the emperor's trumpets flourish thus?
Why are the emperor's trumpets sounding like this?
Belike for joy the emperor hath a son.
Probably for joy that the emperor has a son.
Good morrow, lords. / O, tell me, did you see Aaron the Moor?
Good morning, lords. O, tell me, have you seen Aaron the Moor?
Well, more or less, or ne'er a whit at all, / Here Aaron is; and what with Aaron now?
Well, more or less, or not a bit at all, here Aaron is. And what about Aaron now?
O gentle Aaron, we are all undone! / Now help, or woe betide thee evermore!
O gentle Aaron, we are all ruined! Help now, or misery will fall on you for ever!
Why, what a caterwauling dost thou keep! / What dost thou wrap and fumble in thy arms?
Why, what a caterwauling you are making! What's that you are wrapping and fumbling in your arms?
O, that which I would hide from heaven's eye, / Our empress' shame and stately Rome's disgrace. / She is delivered, lords, she is delivered.
O, something I would hide from heaven's eye: our empress's shame and noble Rome's disgrace. She has been delivered, lords, she has been delivered.
I mean she has given birth.
Well, God give her good rest! What hath he sent her?
Well, God give her a good rest! What has he sent her?
Why, then she is the devil's dam. A joyful issue.
Why, then she is the devil's mother. A happy birth.

A joyless, dismal, black, and sorrowful issue. / Here is the babe, as loathsome as a toad / Amongst the fair-faced breeders of our clime. / The empress sends it thee, thy stamp, thy seal, / And bids thee christen it with thy dagger's point.

A joyless, dreadful, black and sorrowful birth. Here is the baby, as loathsome as a toad among the fair-faced children of our land. The empress sends it to you, your stamp, your seal, and tells you to christen it with the point of your dagger.
Zounds, ye whore, is black so base a hue? / Sweet blowse, you are a beauteous blossom sure.
God's wounds, you whore, is black such a low colour? (To the baby) Sweet chubby-cheeks, you are a beautiful flower for sure.
That which thou canst not undo.
Villain, I have done thy mother.
Villain, I have done your mother.
And therein, hellish dog, thou hast undone her. / Woe to her chance, and damned her loathed choice! / Accursed the offspring of so foul a fiend!
And by doing that, you hellish dog, you have ruined her. Curse her luck, and damn her hateful choice! Cursed be the child of so foul a devil!
Aaron, it must; the mother wills it so.
Aaron, it must. Its mother wants it so.
What, must it, nurse? Then let no man but I / Do execution on my flesh and blood.
What, must it, nurse? Then let no one but me put my own flesh and blood to death.
I'll broach the tadpole on my rapier's point. / Nurse, give it me; my sword shall soon dispatch it.
I'll spit the tadpole on the point of my sword. Nurse, give it to me. My sword will soon finish it off.
Sooner this sword shall plough thy bowels up.
This sword will plough up your guts first.

Stay, murderous villains, will you kill your brother? / Now, by the burning tapers of the sky / That shone so brightly when this boy was got, / He dies upon my scimitar's sharp point / That touches this my first-born son and heir. / I tell you, younglings, not Enceladus, / With all his threatening band of Typhon's brood, / Nor great Alcides, nor the god of war, / Shall seize this prey out of his father's hands. / What, what, ye sanguine, shallow-hearted boys! / Ye white-limed walls, ye alehouse-painted signs! / Coal-black is better than another hue / In that it scorns to bear another hue; / For all the water in the ocean / Can never turn the swan's black legs to white, / Although she lave them hourly in the flood. / Tell the empress from me, I am of age / To keep mine own, excuse it how she can.

Stop, murderous villains, would you kill your brother? Now, by the burning candles of the sky that shone so brightly when this boy was conceived, whoever touches my first-born son and heir dies on the sharp point of my scimitar. I tell you, youngsters, not Enceladus with all his threatening gang of giants, not great Hercules, not the god of war himself, shall snatch this prey out of his father's hands. What, what, you red-faced, shallow-hearted boys! You whitewashed walls, you painted alehouse signs! Coal-black is better than any other colour, because it refuses to take on any other colour. For all the water in the ocean can never turn the swan's black legs white, though she washes them in the waves every hour. Tell the empress from me that I am old enough to keep what is mine. Let her explain it however she can.
Wilt thou betray thy noble mistress thus?
Will you betray your noble mistress like this?

My mistress is my mistress; this my self; / The vigour and the picture of my youth. / This before all the world do I prefer; / This maugre all the world will I keep safe, / Or some of you shall smoke for it in Rome.

My mistress is my mistress; this is myself, the strength and image of my youth. I put this before all the world. I will keep this safe in spite of all the world, or some of you will burn for it in Rome.
By this our mother is for ever shamed.
Our mother is shamed for ever by this.
Rome will despise her for this foul escape.
Rome will despise her for this foul slip.
The emperor in his rage will doom her death.
The emperor in his rage will sentence her to death.
I blush to think upon this ignomy.
I blush to think of this disgrace.

Why, there's the privilege your beauty bears. / Fie, treacherous hue, that will betray with blushing / The close enacts and counsels of thy heart! / Here's a young lad framed of another leer. / Look how the black slave smiles upon the father, / As who should say "Old lad, I am thine own." / He is your brother, lords, sensibly fed / Of that self blood that first gave life to you; / And from your womb where you imprisoned were / He is enfranchised and come to light. / Nay, he is your brother by the surer side, / Although my seal be stamped in his face.

Why, that's the privilege your fair skin gives you. Shame on that treacherous colour, which betrays the secret deeds and thoughts of your heart by blushing! Here's a young lad of a different complexion. Look how the black rascal smiles at his father, as if to say, 'Old lad, I am your own.' He is your brother, lords, plainly fed by the same blood that first gave you life, and he has been set free from the same womb where you were imprisoned and has come into the light. Indeed, he is your brother on the surer side, his mother's, though my seal is stamped on his face.
Aaron, what shall I say unto the empress?
Aaron, what shall I tell the empress?
Advise thee, Aaron, what is to be done, / And we will all subscribe to thy advice. / Save thou the child, so we may all be safe.
Think, Aaron, what must be done, and we will all agree to your advice. Save the child, as long as we can all be safe.
Then sit we down, and let us all consult. / My son and I will have the wind of you. / Keep there. Now talk at pleasure of your safety.
Then let's sit down and all discuss it. My son and I will keep downwind of you. Stay there. Now talk as you please about your safety.
How many women saw this child of his?
How many women saw this child of his?

Why, so, brave lords! When we join in league, / I am a lamb; but if you brave the Moor, / The chafed boar, the mountain lioness, / The ocean swells not so as Aaron storms. / But say again, how many saw the child?

Why, that's the way, brave lords! When we join together, I am a lamb. But if you defy the Moor, the angry boar, the mountain lioness and the swelling ocean do not rage as Aaron does. But tell me again, how many saw the child?
Cornelia the midwife and myself, / And no one else but the delivered empress.
Cornelia the midwife and I, and no one else except the empress who gave birth.
The empress, the midwife, and yourself. / Two may keep counsel when the third's away. / Go to the empress; tell her this I said.
The empress, the midwife and yourself. Two can keep a secret when the third is gone. Go to the empress, and tell her I said this.
"Wheak, wheak!" So cries a pig prepared to the spit.
'Wheak, wheak!' That's how a pig squeals when it's put on the spit.
What mean'st thou, Aaron? Wherefore didst thou this?
What do you mean, Aaron? Why did you do this?

O Lord, sir, 'tis a deed of policy. / Shall she live to betray this guilt of ours, / A long-tongued babbling gossip? No, lords, no. / And now be it known to you my full intent. / Not far, one Muliteus lives, my countryman; / His wife but yesternight was brought to bed. / His child is like to her, fair as you are. / Go pack with him, and give the mother gold, / And tell them both the circumstance of all, / And how by this their child shall be advanced, / And be received for the emperor's heir, / And substituted in the place of mine, / To calm this tempest whirling in the court; / And let the emperor dandle him for his own. / Hark ye, lords; ye see I have given her physic,

O Lord, sir, it was a deed of good sense. Should she live to betray our guilt, a long-tongued, babbling gossip? No, lords, no. And now let me tell you my whole plan. Not far from here lives a countryman of mine called Muliteus. His wife gave birth only last night. Their child looks like her, as fair as you are. Go and do a deal with him. Give the mother gold, tell them both the whole story, and how their child will be raised up by this and accepted as the emperor's heir, put in the place of mine, to calm this storm whirling round the court. And let the emperor dandle him as his own. Listen, lords. You see I have given her medicine,

And you must needs bestow her funeral; / The fields are near, and you are gallant grooms. / This done, see that you take no longer days, / But send the midwife presently to me. / The midwife and the nurse well made away, / Then let the ladies tattle what they please.

and you must give her a funeral. The fields are near, and you are fine strong lads. When that's done, don't waste any time, but send the midwife to me at once. Once the midwife and the nurse are well out of the way, let the ladies gossip as much as they like.
Aaron, I see thou wilt not trust the air / With secrets.
Aaron, I see you won't even trust the air with secrets.
For this care of Tamora, / Herself and hers are highly bound to thee.
For this care of Tamora, she and her family owe you a great deal.

Now to the Goths, as swift as swallow flies, / There to dispose this treasure in mine arms, / And secretly to greet the empress' friends. / Come on, you thick-lipped slave, I'll bear you hence; / For it is you that puts us to our shifts. / I'll make you feed on berries and on roots, / And feed on curds and whey, and suck the goat, / And cabin in a cave, and bring you up / To be a warrior and command a camp.

Now to the Goths, as fast as a swallow flies, to take care of this treasure in my arms and secretly greet the empress's friends. Come on, you thick-lipped rascal, I'll carry you away, for it is you who forces us into these tricks. I'll make you live on berries and roots, on curds and whey, and suck at a goat, and live in a cave, and I'll bring you up to be a warrior and command an army.

Come, Marcus, come. Kinsmen, this is the way. / Sir boy, let me see your archery. / Look ye draw home enough, and 'tis there straight. / Terras Astraea reliquit. / Be you remembered, Marcus, she's gone, she's fled. / Sirs, take you to your tools. You, cousins, shall / Go sound the ocean and cast your nets; / Happily you may catch her in the sea; / Yet there's as little justice as at land. / No; Publius and Sempronius, you must do it; / 'Tis you must dig with mattock and with spade, / And pierce the inmost centre of the earth. / Then, when you come to Pluto's region, / I pray you, deliver him this petition; / Tell him it is for justice and for aid, / And that it comes from old Andronicus, / Shaken with sorrows in ungrateful Rome. / Ah, Rome! Well, well, I made thee miserable / What time I threw the people's suffrages / On him that thus doth tyrannize o'er me. / Go, get you gone; and pray be careful all, / And leave you not a man-of-war unsearched. / This wicked emperor may have shipped her hence; / And, kinsmen, then we may go pipe for justice.

Come, Marcus, come. Kinsmen, this is the way. Young sir, let me see your archery. Make sure you draw the bow back far enough, and it will go straight there. 'Astraea has left the earth.' Remember, Marcus, she's gone, she's fled. Sirs, take up your tools. You, kinsmen, go and sound the depths of the ocean and cast your nets. Perhaps you may catch her in the sea, though there is as little justice there as on land. No, Publius and Sempronius, you must do it. You must dig with pick and spade and bore into the very centre of the earth. Then, when you reach Pluto's kingdom, please give him this petition. Tell him it is for justice and help, and that it comes from old Andronicus, shaken with sorrows in ungrateful Rome. Ah, Rome! Well, well, I made you miserable when I threw the people's votes to the man who now tyrannises over me like this. Go, off you go, and please, all of you, be careful, and don't leave a warship unsearched. This wicked emperor may have shipped her away, and then, kinsmen, we can whistle for justice.
O Publius, is not this a heavy case, / To see thy noble uncle thus distract?
O Publius, isn't this a sad case, to see your noble uncle so distracted?
Therefore, my lords, it highly us concerns / By day and night to attend him carefully, / And feed his humour kindly as we may, / Till time beget some careful remedy.
That is why, my lords, it is important for us to watch over him carefully day and night, and humour him as kindly as we can, until time brings some remedy for his cares.
Kinsmen, his sorrows are past remedy, / But . . . . / Join with the Goths, and with revengeful war / Take wreak on Rome for this ingratitude, / And vengeance on the traitor Saturnine.
Kinsmen, his sorrows are past cure. But (a line is missing here) join with the Goths, and with a war of revenge punish Rome for this ingratitude, and take vengeance on the traitor Saturnine.
Publius, how now? How now, my masters? / What, have you met with her?
Publius, well? Well, my good men? What, have you found her?

No, my good lord; but Pluto sends you word, / If you will have Revenge from hell, you shall. / Marry, for Justice, she is so employed, / He thinks, with Jove in heaven, or somewhere else, / So that perforce you must needs stay a time.

No, my good lord, but Pluto sends you word that if you want Revenge from hell, you shall have it. As for Justice, he thinks she is busy with Jove in heaven, or somewhere else, so you must wait a while.

He doth me wrong to feed me with delays. / I'll dive into the burning lake below, / And pull her out of Acheron by the heels. / Marcus, we are but shrubs, no cedars we, / No big-boned men framed of the Cyclops' size; / But metal, Marcus, steel to the very back, / Yet wrung with wrongs more than our backs can bear; / And sith there's no justice in earth nor hell, / We will solicit heaven and move the gods / To send down Justice for to wreak our wrongs. / Come, to this gear. You are a good archer, Marcus.

He wrongs me by fobbing me off with delays. I'll dive into the burning lake down there and pull her out of the river Acheron by the heels. Marcus, we are only shrubs, not cedars, not big-boned men built to the size of the Cyclops. But we are metal, Marcus, steel right through to the back, and yet weighed down with more wrongs than our backs can bear. And since there is no justice on earth or in hell, we will petition heaven and move the gods to send Justice down to avenge our wrongs. Come, to work. You are a good archer, Marcus.

"Ad Jovem," that's for you; here, "Ad Apollinem"; / "Ad Martem," that's for myself; / Here, boy, "to Pallas"; here, "to Mercury"; / "To Saturn," Caius, not to Saturnine; / You were as good to shoot against the wind. / To it, boy.—Marcus, loose when I bid.— / Of my word, I have written to effect; / There's not a god left unsolicited.

'To Jove,' that's for you. Here, 'To Apollo.' 'To Mars,' that's for myself. Here, boy, 'To Pallas.' Here, 'To Mercury.' 'To Saturn,' Caius, not to Saturnine: you might as well shoot against the wind. Go on, boy. Marcus, let fly when I say. On my word, I have written to the purpose. There's not a god left unasked.
Kinsmen, shoot all your shafts into the court. / We will afflict the emperor in his pride.
Kinsmen, shoot all your arrows into the court. We will torment the emperor in his pride.
Now, masters, draw. [They shoot] O, well said, Lucius! / Good boy, in Virgo's lap! Give it Pallas.
Now, masters, draw your bows. (They shoot) O, well done, Lucius! Good boy, right in Virgo's lap! Give it to Pallas.
My lord, I aim a mile beyond the moon. / Your letter is with Jupiter by this.
My lord, I am aiming a mile beyond the moon. Your letter is with Jupiter by now.
Ha! ha! Publius, Publius, what hast thou done? / See, see, thou hast shot off one of Taurus' horns.
Ha, ha! Publius, Publius, what have you done? Look, look, you have shot off one of Taurus's horns.

This was the sport, my lord; when Publius shot, / The Bull, being galled, gave Aries such a knock / That down fell both the Ram's horns in the court; / And who should find them but the empress' villain? / She laughed, and told the Moor he should not choose / But give them to his master for a present.

That was the fun of it, my lord. When Publius shot, the Bull was hurt and gave Aries such a knock that both the Ram's horns fell down into the court. And who should find them but the empress's villain? She laughed, and told the Moor he had no choice but to give them to his master as a present.
Why, there it goes. God give his lordship joy!
Why, there it goes. God give his lordship joy!
News, news from heaven! Marcus, the post is come. / Sirrah, what tidings? Have you any letters? / Shall I have justice? What says Jupiter?
News, news from heaven! Marcus, the messenger has come. Fellow, what news? Have you any letters? Shall I have justice? What does Jupiter say?
Ho, the gibbet-maker? He says that he hath taken them down again, for / the man must not be hanged till the next week.
Oh, the gallows-maker? He says he has taken them down again, because the man isn't to be hanged until next week.
But what says Jupiter, I ask thee?
But what does Jupiter say, I'm asking you?
Alas, sir, I know not Jubiter; I never drank with him in all my life.
Sorry, sir, I don't know Jubiter. I've never had a drink with him in my life.
Why, villain, art not thou the carrier?
Why, you rascal, aren't you the carrier?
Ay, of my pigeons, sir; nothing else.
Yes, of my pigeons, sir. Nothing else.
Why, didst thou not come from heaven?
Why, didn't you come from heaven?

From heaven? Alas, sir, I never came there. God forbid I should be so / bold to press to heaven in my young days. Why, I am going with my / pigeons to the tribunal plebs, to take up a matter of brawl betwixt my / uncle and one of the emperal's men.

From heaven? Oh no, sir, I've never been there. God forbid I should be so bold as to push my way into heaven while I'm young. Why, I'm going with my pigeons to the people's court, to settle a fight between my uncle and one of the emperor's men.
Why, sir, that is as fit as can be to serve for your oration; and let / him deliver the pigeons to the emperor from you.
Why, sir, that is just the thing to serve for your speech. Let him deliver the pigeons to the emperor from you.
Tell me, can you deliver an oration to the emperor with a grace?
Tell me, can you deliver a speech to the emperor gracefully?
Nay, truly, sir, I could never say grace in all my life.
No, honestly, sir, I've never been able to say grace in my life.

Sirrah, come hither. Make no more ado, / But give your pigeons to the emperor. / By me thou shalt have justice at his hands. / Hold, hold; meanwhile here's money for thy charges. / Give me pen and ink. / Sirrah, can you with a grace deliver up a supplication?

Fellow, come here. Don't make any more fuss, but give your pigeons to the emperor. Through me you shall have justice from him. Wait, wait. Meanwhile, here's money for your trouble. Give me pen and ink. Fellow, can you hand over a petition gracefully?

Then here is a supplication for you. And when you come to him, at the / first approach you must kneel; then kiss his foot; then deliver up your / pigeons; and then look for your reward. I'll be at hand, sir; see you / do it bravely.

Then here is a petition for you. And when you come to him, as soon as you approach, you must kneel, then kiss his foot, then hand over your pigeons, and then wait for your reward. I'll be nearby, sir. See that you do it well.
I warrant you, sir; let me alone.
I promise you, sir. Leave it to me.

Sirrah, hast thou a knife? Come let me see it. / Here, Marcus, fold it in the oration; / For thou hast made it like a humble suppliant. / And when thou hast given it to the emperor, / Knock at my door, and tell me what he says.

Fellow, have you a knife? Come, let me see it. Here, Marcus, wrap it up in the speech, for you have written it like a humble petitioner. (To the Clown) And when you have given it to the emperor, knock at my door and tell me what he says.
God be with you, sir; I will.
God be with you, sir. I will.
Come, Marcus, let us go. Publius, follow me.
Come, Marcus, let us go. Publius, follow me.

Why, lords, what wrongs are these! Was ever seen / An emperor in Rome thus overborne, / Troubled, confronted thus; and, for the extent / Of legal justice, used in such contempt? / My lords, you know, as know the mightful gods, / However these disturbers of our peace / Buzz in the people's ears, there naught hath passed / But even with law against the wilful sons / Of old Andronicus.
