And what an if / His sorrows have so overwhelmed his wits? / Shall we be thus afflicted in his wreaks, / His fits, his frenzy, and his bitterness? / And now he writes to heaven for his redress! / See, here's "to Jove," and this "to Mercury," / This "to Apollo," this to the god of war. / Sweet scrolls to fly about the streets of Rome! / What's this but libelling against the senate, / And blazoning our injustice everywhere? / A goodly humour, is it not, my lords? / As who would say, in Rome no justice were. / But if I live, his feigned ecstasies / Shall be no shelter to these outrages; / But he and his shall know that justice lives / In Saturninus' health; whom, if she sleep, / He'll so awake as he in fury shall / Cut off the proud'st conspirator that lives.

Why, lords, what insults are these! Was an emperor in Rome ever so overpowered, troubled and defied, and treated with such contempt for applying lawful justice? My lords, you know, as the mighty gods know, that whatever these disturbers of our peace whisper in the people's ears, nothing has been done except by law against the wilful sons of old Andronicus. And what if his sorrows have overwhelmed his wits? Must we be tormented by his acts of revenge, his fits, his frenzy and his bitterness? And now he writes to heaven for justice! Look, here's one 'To Jove', and this 'To Mercury', this 'To Apollo', this to the god of war. Sweet scrolls to fly about the streets of Rome! What is this but slandering the senate and proclaiming our injustice everywhere? A fine joke, isn't it, my lords? As if to say there is no justice in Rome. But if I live, his pretended madness will not protect these outrages. He and his family shall learn that justice lives in Saturninus's health, and if she sleeps, he will wake her so that in her fury she will cut down the proudest conspirator alive.

My gracious lord, my lovely Saturnine, / Lord of my life, commander of my thoughts, / Calm thee, and bear the faults of Titus' age, / Th' effects of sorrow for his valiant sons, / Whose loss hath pierced him deep and scarred his heart; / And rather comfort his distressed plight / Than prosecute the meanest or the best / For these contempts. [Aside] Why, thus it shall become / High-witted Tamora to gloze with all. / But, Titus, I have touched thee to the quick; / Thy life-blood out, if Aaron now be wise, / Then is all safe, the anchor in the port.

My gracious lord, my lovely Saturnine, lord of my life, ruler of my thoughts, calm yourself, and put up with the faults of Titus's age, the effects of grief for his brave sons, whose loss has pierced him deeply and scarred his heart. Comfort him in his distress, rather than prosecute the lowest or the highest of them for these insults. (Aside) Why, it suits clever Tamora to smooth everyone over like this. But, Titus, I have wounded you to the quick. Once your life-blood is drained, if Aaron is wise now, then all is safe, the anchor is in the harbour.
How now, good fellow, wouldst thou speak with us?
Well, good fellow, do you want to speak with us?
Yes, forsooth, an your mistresship be emperial.
Yes, indeed, if your mistress-ship is emperial.
Empress I am, but yonder sits the emperor.
I am the empress, but there sits the emperor.
'Tis he. God and Saint Stephen give you good e'en. I have brought you a / letter and a couple of pigeons here.
That's him. God and Saint Stephen give you good evening. I've brought you a letter and a couple of pigeons here.
Go take him away, and hang him presently.
Go, take him away and hang him at once.
How much money must I have?
How much money will I get?
Come, sirrah, you must be hanged.
Come, fellow, you must be hanged.
Hanged! by'r Lady, then I have brought up a neck to a fair end.
Hanged! By Our Lady, then I've raised a neck for a fine end.

Despiteful and intolerable wrongs! / Shall I endure this monstrous villainy? / I know from whence this same device proceeds. / May this be borne as if his traitorous sons, / That died by law for murder of our brother, / Have by my means been butchered wrongfully? / Go, drag the villain hither by the hair; / Nor age nor honour shall shape privilege. / For this proud mock I'll be thy slaughterman, / Sly frantic wretch, that holp'st to make me great, / In hope thyself should govern Rome and me.

Spiteful and unbearable insults! Must I put up with this monstrous villainy? I know where this trick comes from. Is this to be borne, as if his treacherous sons, who died lawfully for murdering our brother, had been wrongly butchered on my orders? Go, drag the villain here by the hair. Neither age nor honour shall give him special treatment. For this proud mockery I'll be your executioner, you sly, raving wretch, who helped to make me great in the hope that you would rule Rome and me.
What news do you bring, Aemilius?

Arm, my lord! Rome never had more cause. / The Goths have gathered head, and with a power / Of high-resolved men, bent to the spoil, / They hither march amain, under conduct / Of Lucius, son to old Andronicus; / Who threats, in course of this revenge, to do / As much as ever Coriolanus did.

To arms, my lord! Rome never had more reason. The Goths have raised an army, and with a force of determined men, bent on plunder, they are marching here at full speed, led by Lucius, son of old Andronicus. He threatens, in pursuing this revenge, to do as much as Coriolanus ever did.

Is warlike Lucius general of the Goths? / These tidings nip me, and I hang the head / As flowers with frost, or grass beat down with storms. / Ay, now begins our sorrows to approach. / 'Tis he the common people love so much; / Myself hath often overheard them say, / When I have walked like a private man, / That Lucius' banishment was wrongfully, / And they have wished that Lucius were their emperor.

Is warlike Lucius general of the Goths? This news blights me, and I hang my head like flowers in frost or grass beaten down by storms. Yes, now our sorrows are beginning to close in. He is the one the common people love so much. I have often overheard them say myself, when I have walked about in disguise, that Lucius's banishment was unjust, and they have wished that Lucius were their emperor.
Why should you fear? Is not your city strong?
Why should you be afraid? Isn't your city strong?
Ay, but the citizens favour Lucius, / And will revolt from me to succour him.
Yes, but the citizens favour Lucius, and will rebel against me to help him.

King, be thy thoughts imperious like thy name. / Is the sun dimmed, that gnats do fly in it? / The eagle suffers little birds to sing, / And is not careful what they mean thereby, / Knowing that with the shadow of his wings / He can at pleasure stint their melody; / Even so mayest thou the giddy men of Rome. / Then cheer thy spirit; for know, thou emperor, / I will enchant the old Andronicus / With words more sweet, and yet more dangerous, / Than baits to fish or honey-stalks to sheep, / Whenas the one is wounded with the bait, / The other rotted with delicious feed.

King, let your thoughts be as commanding as your title. Is the sun dimmed because gnats fly in it? The eagle lets little birds sing and does not care what they mean by it, knowing that he can stop their song whenever he likes with the shadow of his wings. You can do the same with the fickle men of Rome. So cheer up. For know, my emperor, I will bewitch old Andronicus with words sweeter, and yet more dangerous, than bait to fish or clover to sheep: the fish is hooked by the bait, and the sheep is made sick by its delicious food.
But he will not entreat his son for us.
But he will not plead with his son for us.

If Tamora entreat him, then he will, / For I can smooth and fill his aged ears / With golden promises, that, were his heart / Almost impregnable, his old ears deaf, / Yet should both ear and heart obey my tongue. / [to Aemilius] Go thou before, be our ambassador. / Say that the emperor requests a parley / Of warlike Lucius, and appoint the meeting / Even at his father's house, the old Andronicus.

If Tamora pleads with him, then he will. For I can flatter him and fill his old ears with golden promises, so that even if his heart were almost impossible to storm and his old ears deaf, both ear and heart would obey my tongue. (To Aemilius) You go ahead and be our ambassador. Say that the emperor asks warlike Lucius for a meeting, and arrange it at his father's house, old Andronicus's.
Aemilius, do this message honourably, / And if he stand on hostage for his safety, / Bid him demand what pledge will please him best.
Aemilius, deliver this message honourably, and if he insists on hostages for his safety, tell him to ask for whatever guarantee will please him best.
Your bidding shall I do effectually.
I will carry out your orders effectively.

Now will I to that old Andronicus, / And temper him with all the art I have, / To pluck proud Lucius from the warlike Goths. / And now, sweet emperor, be blithe again, / And bury all thy fear in my devices.
Now I'll go to old Andronicus and work on him with all my skill, to pull proud Lucius away from the warlike Goths. And now, sweet emperor, be cheerful again, and bury all your fear in my plans.
Then go successantly, and plead to him.
Then go, and may you succeed, and plead with him.

Approved warriors and my faithful friends, / I have received letters from great Rome / Which signifies what hate they bear their emperor / And how desirous of our sight they are. / Therefore, great lords, be, as your titles witness, / Imperious, and impatient of your wrongs; / And wherein Rome hath done you any scath, / Let him make treble satisfaction.

Proven warriors and faithful friends, I have received letters from great Rome which tell me how much they hate their emperor and how eager they are to see us. So, great lords, be what your titles show you to be, commanding and unwilling to put up with wrongs. And wherever Rome has done you harm, let the emperor pay you back three times over.

Brave slip, sprung from the great Andronicus, / Whose name was once our terror, now our comfort, / Whose high exploits and honourable deeds / Ingrateful Rome requites with foul contempt, / Be bold in us. We'll follow where thou lead'st, / Like stinging bees in hottest summer's day / Led by their master to the flowered fields, / And be avenged on cursed Tamora.

Brave offshoot of the great Andronicus, whose name was once our terror and is now our comfort, whose high achievements and honourable deeds ungrateful Rome repays with foul contempt: be confident in us. We'll follow wherever you lead, like stinging bees on the hottest summer's day led by their king to the flowering fields, and take revenge on cursed Tamora.
And as he saith, so say we all with him.
And as he says, so we all say with him.
I humbly thank him, and I thank you all. / But who comes here, led by a lusty Goth?
I humbly thank him, and I thank you all. But who is this, led by a sturdy Goth?

Renowned Lucius, from our troops I strayed / To gaze upon a ruinous monastery; / And as I earnestly did fix mine eye / Upon the wasted building, suddenly / I heard a child cry underneath a wall. / I made unto the noise, when soon I heard / The crying babe controlled with this discourse: / "Peace, tawny slave, half me and half thy dame! / Did not thy hue bewray whose brat thou art, / Had nature lent thee but thy mother's look, / Villain, thou mightst have been an emperor. / But where the bull and cow are both milk-white, / They never do beget a coal-black calf. / Peace, villain, peace!" even thus he rates the babe, / "For I must bear thee to a trusty Goth, / Who, when he knows thou art the empress' babe, / Will hold thee dearly for thy mother's sake." / With this, my weapon drawn, I rushed upon him, / Surprised him suddenly, and brought him hither / To use as you think needful of the man.

Famous Lucius, I wandered away from our troops to look at a ruined monastery. And as I was staring hard at the wrecked building, I suddenly heard a child crying underneath a wall. I went towards the noise, and soon I heard the crying baby being hushed with these words: 'Quiet, brown rascal, half me and half your mother! If your colour didn't give away whose brat you are, if nature had only given you your mother's looks, you villain, you might have been an emperor. But when the bull and cow are both milk-white, they never produce a coal-black calf. Quiet, villain, quiet!' That's how he scolded the baby. 'For I must carry you to a trusty Goth, who, when he knows you are the empress's baby, will treasure you for your mother's sake.' At that, I drew my weapon and rushed at him, took him by surprise, and brought him here for you to deal with as you think necessary.

O worthy Goth, this is the incarnate devil / That robbed Andronicus of his good hand; / This is the pearl that pleased your empress' eye; / And here's the base fruit of her burning lust. / Say, wall-eyed slave, whither wouldst thou convey / This growing image of thy fiend-like face? / Why dost not speak? What, deaf? Not a word? / A halter, soldiers, hang him on this tree, / And by his side his fruit of bastardy.

O worthy Goth, this is the devil in human form who robbed Andronicus of his good hand. This is the pearl that pleased your empress's eye, and here is the low fruit of her burning lust. Tell me, glaring slave, where were you taking this growing copy of your devilish face? Why don't you speak? What, deaf? Not a word? A rope, soldiers. Hang him on this tree, and his bastard beside him.
Touch not the boy, he is of royal blood.
Don't touch the boy. He is of royal blood.
Too like the sire for ever being good. / First hang the child, that he may see it sprawl, / A sight to vex the father's soul withal. / Get me a ladder.
Too like his father ever to be good. Hang the child first, so that he can see it kick, a sight to torment the father's soul. Get me a ladder.

Lucius, save the child; / And bear it from me to the empress. / If thou do this, I'll show thee wondrous things / That highly may advantage thee to hear. / If thou wilt not, befall what may befall, / I'll speak no more but "Vengeance rot you all!"

Lucius, save the child, and take it to the empress for me. If you do this, I'll reveal amazing things that will be very much to your advantage to hear. If you won't, then whatever happens, I'll say nothing more but 'Vengeance rot you all!'
Say on, and if it please me which thou speak'st, / Thy child shall live, and I will see it nourished.
Speak, and if what you say pleases me, your child shall live, and I will see that it is fed and cared for.

And if it please thee? Why, assure thee, Lucius, / 'Twill vex thy soul to hear what I shall speak; / For I must talk of murders, rapes, and massacres, / Acts of black night, abominable deeds, / Complots of mischief, treason, villainies, / Ruthful to hear, yet piteously performed. / And this shall all be buried in my death, / Unless thou swear to me my child shall live.

If it pleases you? Why, I promise you, Lucius, it will torment your soul to hear what I have to say. For I must talk of murders, rapes and massacres, acts of black night, disgusting deeds, plots of evil, treason, villainies, pitiful to hear and yet pitilessly done. And all this will be buried with my death unless you swear to me that my child shall live.
Tell on thy mind; I say thy child shall live.
Say what's on your mind. I tell you your child shall live.
Swear that he shall, and then I will begin.
Swear that he shall, and then I'll begin.
Who should I swear by? Thou believ'st no god. / That granted, how canst thou believe an oath?
What should I swear by? You don't believe in any god. That being so, how can you believe an oath?

What if I do not? As indeed I do not; / Yet, for I know thou art religious, / And hast a thing within thee called conscience, / With twenty popish tricks and ceremonies / Which I have seen thee careful to observe, / Therefore I urge thy oath; for that I know / An idiot holds his bauble for a god, / And keeps the oath which by that god he swears, / To that I'll urge him. Therefore thou shalt vow / By that same god, what god soe'er it be / That thou adorest and hast in reverence, / To save my boy, to nourish and bring him up; / Or else I will discover naught to thee.

What if I don't? And indeed I don't. Yet because I know you are religious, and have a thing inside you called conscience, with twenty popish tricks and ceremonies that I have seen you careful to observe, I insist on your oath. For I know that an idiot takes his jester's stick for a god and keeps the oath he swears by that god, and I'll hold him to it. So you shall swear by that same god, whatever god it is that you worship and revere, to save my boy and feed him and bring him up, or else I will reveal nothing to you.
Even by my god I swear to thee I will.
I swear to you by my god that I will.
First know thou, I begot him on the empress.
First, know that I fathered him on the empress.
O most insatiate and luxurious woman!
O most insatiable and lustful woman!

Tut, Lucius, this was but a deed of charity / To that which thou shalt hear of me anon. / 'Twas her two sons that murdered Bassianus; / They cut thy sister's tongue, and ravished her, / And cut her hands, and trimmed her as thou sawest.

Tut, Lucius, that was only an act of charity compared with what you'll hear from me shortly. It was her two sons who murdered Bassianus. They cut out your sister's tongue and raped her, and cut off her hands, and trimmed her as you saw.
O detestable villain, call'st thou that trimming?
O hateful villain, do you call that trimming?
Why, she was washed, and cut, and trimmed; and 'twas / Trim sport for them which had the doing of it.
Why, she was washed and cut and trimmed, and it was fine sport for the ones who did it.
O barbarous beastly villains, like thyself!
O barbarous, beastly villains, like you!

Indeed, I was their tutor to instruct them. / That codding spirit had they from their mother, / As sure a card as ever won the set; / That bloody mind I think they learned of me, / As true a dog as ever fought at head. / Well, let my deeds be witness of my worth. / I trained thy brethren to that guileful hole / Where the dead corpse of Bassianus lay. / I wrote the letter that thy father found, / And hid the gold within that letter mentioned, / Confederate with the queen and her two sons. / And what not done, that thou hast cause to rue, / Wherein I had no stroke of mischief in't? / I played the cheater for thy father's hand, / And, when I had it, drew myself apart, / And almost broke my heart with extreme laughter. / I pried me through the crevice of a wall / When, for his hand, he had his two sons' heads; / Beheld his tears, and laughed so heartily / That both mine eyes were rainy like to his. / And when I told the empress of this sport, / She sounded almost at my pleasing tale, / And for my tidings gave me twenty kisses.

Indeed, I was their tutor and taught them. They got that lustful spirit from their mother, as sure a card as ever won the game. That bloody mind I think they learned from me, as true a dog as ever went for the bull's head. Well, let my deeds prove what I am worth. I lured your brothers to that treacherous hole where the dead body of Bassianus lay. I wrote the letter your father found and hid the gold that the letter mentioned, in league with the queen and her two sons. And what has been done that you have cause to grieve over, in which I did not have a hand in the mischief? I tricked your father out of his hand, and when I had it, I went off on my own and almost broke my heart with laughing. I peeped through a crack in a wall when he got his two sons' heads in return for his hand. I watched his tears and laughed so heartily that both my eyes were as wet as his. And when I told the empress about this sport, she almost fainted at my pleasing story, and gave me twenty kisses for my news.
What, canst thou say all this and never blush?
What, can you say all this and never blush?
Ay, like a black dog, as the saying is.
Yes, like a black dog, as the saying goes.
Art thou not sorry for these heinous deeds?
Aren't you sorry for these terrible deeds?

Ay, that I had not done a thousand more. / Even now I curse the day, and yet, I think, / Few come within the compass of my curse, / Wherein I did not some notorious ill, / As kill a man, or else devise his death; / Ravish a maid, or plot the way to do it; / Accuse some innocent, and forswear myself; / Set deadly enmity between two friends; / Make poor men's cattle break their necks; / Set fire on barns and haystalks in the night, / And bid the owners quench them with their tears. / Oft have I digged up dead men from their graves, / And set them upright at their dear friends' door, / Even when their sorrows almost was forgot, / And on their skins, as on the bark of trees, / Have with my knife carved in Roman letters, / "Let not your sorrow die, though I am dead." / But I have done a thousand dreadful things / As willingly as one would kill a fly, / And nothing grieves me heartily indeed / But that I cannot do ten thousand more.

Yes: sorry that I didn't do a thousand more. Even now I curse the day (and yet I think few days come within reach of my curse) in which I did not do some notorious evil: killed a man or plotted his death, raped a girl or planned how to do it, accused some innocent person and swore falsely, set deadly hatred between two friends, made poor men's cattle break their necks, set fire to barns and haystacks at night and told the owners to put them out with their tears. I have often dug dead men up from their graves and stood them upright at their dear friends' doors, just when their grief was almost forgotten, and carved on their skins with my knife, as on the bark of trees, in Roman letters: 'Let not your sorrow die, though I am dead.' Oh, I have done a thousand dreadful things as willingly as one would kill a fly, and nothing really grieves me except that I cannot do ten thousand more.
Bring down the devil, for he must not die / So sweet a death as hanging presently.
Bring the devil down, for he must not die such a sweet death as a quick hanging.
If there be devils, would I were a devil, / To live and burn in everlasting fire, / So I might have your company in hell / But to torment you with my bitter tongue!
If there are devils, I wish I were a devil, to live and burn in everlasting fire, if only I could have your company in hell to torment you with my bitter tongue!
Sirs, stop his mouth, and let him speak no more.
Sirs, gag him, and let him speak no more.
My lord, there is a messenger from Rome / Desires to be admitted to your presence.
My lord, there is a messenger from Rome who asks to be let in to see you.
Let him come near. / Welcome, Aemilius. What's the news from Rome?
Let him come forward. Welcome, Aemilius. What's the news from Rome?

Lord Lucius, and you princes of the Goths, / The Roman emperor greets you all by me; / And, for he understands you are in arms, / He craves a parley at your father's house, / Willing you to demand your hostages, / And they shall be immediately delivered.

Lord Lucius, and you princes of the Goths, the Roman emperor greets you all through me. And because he understands you are armed for war, he asks for a meeting at your father's house. He invites you to name your hostages, and they will be handed over immediately.
Aemilius, let the emperor give his pledges / Unto my father and my uncle Marcus, / And we will come. March away.
Aemilius, let the emperor give his hostages to my father and my uncle Marcus, and we will come. March on.

Thus, in this strange and sad habiliment, / I will encounter with Andronicus, / And say I am Revenge, sent from below / To join with him and right his heinous wrongs. / Knock at his study, where they say he keeps / To ruminate strange plots of dire revenge; / Tell him Revenge is come to join with him / And work confusion on his enemies.

In this strange and sombre costume, I will meet Andronicus and say I am Revenge, sent up from the underworld to join with him and avenge his terrible wrongs. Knock at his study, where they say he stays to brood over strange plots of dreadful revenge. Tell him Revenge has come to join with him and bring ruin on his enemies.

Who doth molest my contemplation? / Is it your trick to make me ope the door, / That so my sad decrees may fly away / And all my study be to no effect? / You are deceived; for what I mean to do / See here in bloody lines I have set down; / And what is written shall be executed.

Who is disturbing my thoughts? Is it your trick to make me open the door, so that my sad decisions fly away and all my study comes to nothing? You are wrong. For see, I have written down here in lines of blood what I mean to do, and what is written shall be carried out.
Titus, I am come to talk with thee.
Titus, I have come to talk with you.
No, not a word; how can I grace my talk, / Wanting a hand to give it action? / Thou hast the odds of me; therefore no more.
No, not a word. How can I give my words grace without a hand to make gestures? You have the advantage of me, so no more.
If thou didst know me, thou wouldst talk with me.
If you knew who I was, you would talk with me.

I am not mad; I know thee well enough. / Witness this wretched stump, witness these crimson lines; / Witness these trenches made by grief and care; / Witness the tiring day and heavy night; / Witness all sorrow that I know thee well / For our proud empress, mighty Tamora. / Is not thy coming for my other hand?

I am not mad. I know you well enough. This wretched stump bears witness, these crimson lines bear witness, these furrows made by grief and care bear witness, the tiring day and the heavy night bear witness, all sorrow bears witness that I know you well: you are our proud empress, mighty Tamora. Haven't you come for my other hand?

Know thou, sad man, I am not Tamora; / She is thy enemy, and I thy friend. / I am Revenge, sent from th' infernal kingdom / To ease the gnawing vulture of thy mind / By working wreakful vengeance on thy foes. / Come down and welcome me to this world's light; / Confer with me of murder and of death. / There's not a hollow cave or lurking-place, / No vast obscurity or misty vale, / Where bloody murder or detested rape / Can couch for fear but I will find them out, / And in their ears tell them my dreadful name, / Revenge, which makes the foul offender quake.

Know, sad man, that I am not Tamora. She is your enemy, and I am your friend. I am Revenge, sent from the kingdom of hell to ease the vulture gnawing at your mind by taking furious vengeance on your enemies. Come down and welcome me to the light of this world. Talk with me of murder and death. There is no hollow cave or hiding place, no vast darkness or misty valley, where bloody murder or hateful rape can crouch in fear, that I will not find them out and tell them my dreadful name in their ears: Revenge, which makes the foul offender tremble.
Art thou Revenge? And art thou sent to me / To be a torment to mine enemies?
Are you Revenge? And are you sent to me to be a torment to my enemies?
I am; therefore come down and welcome me.
I am. So come down and welcome me.

Do me some service ere I come to thee. / Lo, by thy side where Rape and Murder stands; / Now give some surance that thou art Revenge: / Stab them, or tear them on thy chariot wheels, / And then I'll come and be thy waggoner, / And whirl along with thee about the globe. / Provide thee two proper palfreys, black as jet, / To hale thy vengeful waggon swift away, / And find out murderers in their guilty caves. / And when thy car is loaden with their heads, / I will dismount, and by the waggon-wheel / Trot like a servile footman all day long, / Even from Hyperion's rising in the east / Until his very downfall in the sea. / And day by day I'll do this heavy task, / So thou destroy Rapine and Murder there.

Do me some service before I come to you. Look, beside you stand Rape and Murder. Now give me some proof that you are Revenge. Stab them, or tear them apart on your chariot wheels, and then I'll come and be your driver and whirl round the world with you. Get yourself two fine horses, black as jet, to pull your chariot of vengeance swiftly away and find murderers in their guilty caves. And when your chariot is loaded with their heads, I will get down and trot beside the wheel like a humble servant all day long, from the moment the sun rises in the east until it sinks into the sea. And I'll do this heavy task day after day, if you destroy Rape and Murder there.
These are my ministers, and come with me.
These are my servants, and they come with me.
Are they thy ministers? What are they called?
Are they your servants? What are they called?
Rapine and Murder; therefore called so / 'Cause they take vengeance of such kind of men.
Rape and Murder, called so because they take revenge on men of that kind.

Good Lord, how like the empress' sons they are, / And you the empress! But we worldly men / Have miserable, mad, mistaking eyes. / O sweet Revenge, now do I come to thee; / And, if one arm's embracement will content thee, / I will embrace thee in it by and by.

Good Lord, how like the empress's sons they are, and you like the empress! But we mortal men have miserable, mad, mistaken eyes. O sweet Revenge, now I am coming to you, and if a one-armed hug will satisfy you, I will hug you with it in a moment.

This closing with him fits his lunacy. / Whate'er I forge to feed his brain-sick humours, / Do you uphold and maintain in your speeches, / For now he firmly takes me for Revenge; / And, being credulous in this mad thought, / I'll make him send for Lucius his son; / And whilst I at a banquet hold him sure, / I'll find some cunning practice out of hand / To scatter and disperse the giddy Goths, / Or, at the least, make them his enemies. / See, here he comes, and I must ply my theme.

Going along with him like this suits his madness. Whatever I invent to feed his sick fancies, you back it up and keep it going in what you say. For now he firmly takes me for Revenge, and since he believes this mad idea, I'll make him send for his son Lucius. And while I keep him safely occupied at a banquet, I'll quickly find some clever trick to scatter and break up the fickle Goths, or at least turn them against him. Look, here he comes, and I must keep up my part.

Long have I been forlorn, and all for thee. / Welcome, dread Fury, to my woeful house. / Rapine and Murder, you are welcome too. / How like the empress and her sons you are! / Well are you fitted, had you but a Moor. / Could not all hell afford you such a devil? / For well I wot the empress never wags / But in her company there is a Moor; / And, would you represent our queen aright, / It were convenient you had such a devil. / But welcome as you are. What shall we do?

I have been lonely a long time, and all for you. Welcome, dreadful Fury, to my house of sorrow. Rape and Murder, you are welcome too. How like the empress and her sons you are! Your costumes would be complete if only you had a Moor. Couldn't all hell provide you with such a devil? For I know very well the empress never stirs without a Moor in her company, and if you want to play our queen properly, you ought to have such a devil. But welcome as you are. What shall we do?
What wouldst thou have us do, Andronicus?
What would you have us do, Andronicus?
Show me a murderer, I'll deal with him.
Show me a murderer, and I'll deal with him.
Show me a villain that hath done a rape, / And I am sent to be revenged on him.
Show me a villain who has committed rape, and I am sent to take revenge on him.
Show me a thousand that hath done thee wrong, / And I will be revenged on them all.
Show me a thousand who have wronged you, and I will take revenge on them all.

Look round about the wicked streets of Rome, / And when thou find'st a man that's like thyself, / Good Murder, stab him; he's a murderer. / Go thou with him; and when it is thy hap / To find another that is like to thee, / Good Rapine, stab him; he is a ravisher. / Go thou with them; and in the emperor's court / There is a queen, attended by a Moor; / Well shalt thou know her by thine own proportion, / For up and down she doth resemble thee. / I pray thee, do on them some violent death; / They have been violent to me and mine.

Look all round the wicked streets of Rome, and when you find a man who looks like you, good Murder, stab him: he's a murderer. (To Chiron) You go with him, and when you happen to find another who looks like you, good Rape, stab him: he is a rapist. (To Tamora) You go with them. In the emperor's court there is a queen, attended by a Moor. You'll recognise her easily by your own shape, for she looks exactly like you in every way. Please give them some violent death. They have been violent to me and my family.

Well hast thou lessoned us; this shall we do. / But would it please thee, good Andronicus, / To send for Lucius, thy thrice-valiant son, / Who leads towards Rome a band of warlike Goths, / And bid him come and banquet at thy house? / When he is here, even at thy solemn feast, / I will bring in the empress and her sons, / The emperor himself, and all thy foes, / And at thy mercy shall they stoop and kneel, / And on them shalt thou ease thy angry heart. / What says Andronicus to this device?

You have taught us well. We shall do this. But would you be so good, Andronicus, as to send for Lucius, your thrice-brave son, who is leading an army of warlike Goths towards Rome, and invite him to come and feast at your house? When he is here, at your solemn feast, I will bring in the empress and her sons, the emperor himself, and all your enemies, and they shall bow and kneel at your mercy, and you can take out your angry heart on them. What does Andronicus say to this plan?
Marcus, my brother, 'tis sad Titus calls.
Marcus, my brother, it is sad Titus calling.

Go, gentle Marcus, to thy nephew Lucius; / Thou shalt inquire him out among the Goths. / Bid him repair to me and bring with him / Some of the chiefest princes of the Goths; / Bid him encamp his soldiers where they are. / Tell him the emperor and the empress too / Feast at my house, and he shall feast with them. / This do thou for my love; and so let him, / As he regards his aged father's life.

Go, gentle Marcus, to your nephew Lucius. You must seek him out among the Goths. Tell him to come to me and bring some of the leading princes of the Goths with him. Tell him to keep his soldiers camped where they are. Tell him the emperor and the empress are feasting at my house, and he shall feast with them. Do this for love of me, and let him do it, as he values his old father's life.
This will I do, and soon return again.
I'll do this, and come back soon.
Now will I hence about thy business, / And take my ministers along with me.
Now I'll go and see to your business, and take my servants with me.
Nay, nay, let Rape and Murder stay with me, / Or else I'll call my brother back again / And cleave to no revenge but Lucius.
No, no, let Rape and Murder stay with me, or else I'll call my brother back and rely on no revenge but Lucius.

[Aside to them] What say you, boys? Will you abide with him, / Whiles I go tell my lord the emperor / How I have governed our determined jest? / Yield to his humour, smooth and speak him fair, / And tarry with him till I come again.

(Aside to her sons) What do you say, boys? Will you stay with him while I go and tell my lord the emperor how I have managed the joke we planned? Go along with his whims, flatter him and speak kindly to him, and stay with him until I come back.
[Aside] I knew them all, though they suppose me mad, / And will o'erreach them in their own devices, / A pair of cursed hell-hounds and their dam.
(Aside) I recognised them all, though they think I'm mad, and I'll outwit them in their own schemes: a pair of cursed hellhounds and their mother.
Madam, depart at pleasure; leave us here.
Madam, go when you like. Leave us here.
Farewell, Andronicus. Revenge now goes / To lay a complot to betray thy foes.
Farewell, Andronicus. Revenge is going now to lay a plot to trap your enemies.
I know thou dost; and, sweet Revenge, farewell.
I know you are. And, sweet Revenge, farewell.
Tell us, old man, how shall we be employed?
Tell us, old man, what shall we do?
Tut, I have work enough for you to do. / Publius, come hither, Caius, and Valentine.
Tut, I have plenty of work for you to do. Publius, come here, and Caius, and Valentine.
The empress' sons, I take them, Chiron, Demetrius.
The empress's sons, I think: Chiron and Demetrius.

Fie, Publius, fie, thou art too much deceived. / The one is Murder, and Rape is the other's name; / And therefore bind them, gentle Publius. / Caius and Valentine, lay hands on them. / Oft have you heard me wish for such an hour, / And now I find it. Therefore bind them sure, / And stop their mouths if they begin to cry.

Shame on you, Publius, you are badly mistaken. One is Murder, and the other's name is Rape. So tie them up, gentle Publius. Caius and Valentine, seize them. You have often heard me wish for an hour like this, and now I have found it. So tie them up tightly, and gag them if they start to shout.
Villains, forbear! We are the empress' sons.
Villains, stop! We are the empress's sons.
And therefore do we what we are commanded. / Stop close their mouths, let them not speak a word. / Is he sure bound? Look that you bind them fast.
And that is why we are doing what we are told. Gag them tightly; don't let them say a word. Is he tied securely? Make sure you bind them fast.

Come, come, Lavinia; look, thy foes are bound. / Sirs, stop their mouths, let them not speak to me, / But let them hear what fearful words I utter. / O villains, Chiron and Demetrius! / Here stands the spring whom you have stained with mud, / This goodly summer with your winter mixed. / You killed her husband, and for that vile fault / Two of her brothers were condemned to death, / My hand cut off and made a merry jest, / Both her sweet hands, her tongue, and that more dear / Than hands or tongue, her spotless chastity, / Inhuman traitors, you constrained and forced. / What would you say if I should let you speak? / Villains, for shame you could not beg for grace. / Hark, wretches, how I mean to martyr you. / This one hand yet is left to cut your throats, / Whiles that Lavinia 'tween her stumps doth hold / The basin that receives your guilty blood. / You know your mother means to feast with me, / And calls herself Revenge, and thinks me mad. / Hark, villains! I will grind your bones to dust, / And with your blood and it I'll make a paste, / And of the paste a coffin I will rear, / And make two pasties of your shameful heads, / And bid that strumpet, your unhallowed dam, / Like to the earth swallow her own increase. / This is the feast that I have bid her to, / And this the banquet she shall surfeit on; / For worse than Philomel you used my daughter, / And worse than Procne I will be revenged. / And now prepare your throats.—Lavinia, come / Receive the blood.

Come, come, Lavinia. Look, your enemies are tied up. Sirs, gag them. Don't let them speak to me, but let them hear the fearful words I say. O villains, Chiron and Demetrius! Here stands the fountain you have fouled with mud, this fine summer you have mixed with your winter. You killed her husband, and for that vile crime two of her brothers were condemned to death, my hand was cut off and made into a merry joke. Both her sweet hands, her tongue, and, dearer than hands or tongue, her spotless chastity, you inhuman traitors, you took by force. What would you say if I let you speak? Villains, for shame you could not beg for mercy. Listen, wretches, to how I mean to torture you. This one hand is still left to cut your throats, while Lavinia holds between her stumps the basin that catches your guilty blood. You know your mother means to feast with me. She calls herself Revenge, and thinks I'm mad. Listen, villains! I will grind your bones to dust, and make a paste of it with your blood, and with the paste I'll build a pie crust, and make two pies of your shameful heads. And I'll invite that whore, your unholy mother, to swallow her own children, as the earth does. This is the feast I have invited her to, and this is the banquet she will gorge on. For you treated my daughter worse than Philomela was treated, and I will take worse revenge than Procne. And now get your throats ready. Lavinia, come, catch the blood.

And when that they are dead, / Let me go grind their bones to powder small, / And with this hateful liquor temper it, / And in that paste let their vile heads be baked. / Come, come, be everyone officious / To make this banquet, which I wish may prove / More stern and bloody than the Centaurs' feast. / So, now bring them in, for I'll play the cook, / And see them ready against their mother comes.

And when they are dead, let me go and grind their bones to fine powder, and mix it with this hateful liquid, and let their vile heads be baked in that paste. Come, come, everyone, be busy making this banquet, which I hope will prove grimmer and bloodier than the Centaurs' feast. So, now bring them in, for I'll play the cook and have them ready for when their mother comes.
Uncle Marcus, since 'tis my father's mind / That I repair to Rome, I am content.
Uncle Marcus, since it is my father's wish that I go to Rome, I am content.
And ours with thine, befall what fortune will.
And we go with you, whatever fortune brings.

Good uncle, take you in this barbarous Moor, / This ravenous tiger, this accursed devil; / Let him receive no sust'nance, fetter him, / Till he be brought unto the empress' face / For testimony of her foul proceedings. / And see the ambush of our friends be strong; / I fear the emperor means no good to us.

Good uncle, take this barbarous Moor inside, this greedy tiger, this cursed devil. Give him no food, chain him up, until he is brought face to face with the empress as evidence of her foul doings. And see that our friends lying in ambush are strong. I am afraid the emperor means us no good.
Some devil whisper curses in my ear, / And prompt me that my tongue may utter forth / The venomous malice of my swelling heart!
May some devil whisper curses in my ear and prompt me, so that my tongue can pour out the poisonous malice of my swelling heart!
Away, inhuman dog, unhallowed slave! / Sirs, help our uncle to convey him in.
Away, inhuman dog, unholy slave! Sirs, help our uncle to take him in.
The trumpets show the emperor is at hand.
The trumpets show the emperor is close by.
What, hath the firmament more suns than one?
What, does the sky have more than one sun?
What boots it thee to call thyself a sun?
What good does it do you to call yourself a sun?

Rome's emperor, and nephew, break the parle; / These quarrels must be quietly debated. / The feast is ready which the careful Titus / Hath ordained to an honourable end, / For peace, for love, for league, and good to Rome. / Please you, therefore, draw nigh and take your places.

Emperor of Rome, and nephew, stop this argument. These quarrels must be settled calmly. The feast is ready, which careful Titus has arranged for an honourable purpose: for peace, for love, for alliance and for the good of Rome. So please come forward and take your places.
Welcome, my lord; welcome, dread queen; / Welcome, ye warlike Goths; welcome, Lucius; / And welcome all. Although the cheer be poor, / 'Twill fill your stomachs; please you eat of it.
Welcome, my lord. Welcome, dread queen. Welcome, you warlike Goths. Welcome, Lucius. And welcome all. Though the food is poor, it will fill your stomachs. Please eat.
Why art thou thus attired, Andronicus?
Why are you dressed like this, Andronicus?
Because I would be sure to have all well / To entertain your highness and your empress.
Because I wanted to be sure everything was right for entertaining your highness and your empress.
We are beholden to you, good Andronicus.
We are grateful to you, good Andronicus.

An if your highness knew my heart, you were. / My lord the emperor, resolve me this: / Was it well done of rash Virginius / To slay his daughter with his own right hand, / Because she was enforced, stained, and deflowered?

If your highness knew my heart, you would be. My lord the emperor, answer me this. Did hot-headed Virginius do right to kill his daughter with his own right hand because she had been raped, stained and robbed of her virginity?
Because the girl should not survive her shame, / And by her presence still renew his sorrows.
Because the girl should not outlive her shame, and keep renewing his sorrows by being there.

A reason mighty, strong, and effectual; / A pattern, precedent, and lively warrant / For me, most wretched, to perform the like. / Die, die, Lavinia, and thy shame with thee; / And with thy shame thy father's sorrow die!

A mighty, strong and convincing reason: a model, a precedent and a living warrant for me, most wretched man, to do the same. Die, die, Lavinia, and your shame with you, and with your shame let your father's sorrow die!
What hast thou done, unnatural and unkind?
What have you done, you unnatural, cruel man?
Killed her for whom my tears have made me blind. / I am as woeful as Virginius was, / And have a thousand times more cause than he / To do this outrage, and it now is done.
Killed her for whom my tears have made me blind. I am as miserable as Virginius was, and I have a thousand times more reason than he had to do this violent thing, and now it is done.
What, was she ravished? Tell who did the deed.
What, was she raped? Tell us who did it.
Will't please you eat? Will't please your highness feed?
Won't you eat? Won't your highness have something?
Why hast thou slain thine only daughter thus?
Why have you killed your only daughter like this?
Not I; 'twas Chiron and Demetrius. / They ravished her, and cut away her tongue; / And they, 'twas they, that did her all this wrong.
Not I: it was Chiron and Demetrius. They raped her and cut out her tongue, and it was they, they, who did her all this wrong.
Go fetch them hither to us presently.
Go and fetch them here to us at once.
Why, there they are, both baked in that pie, / Whereof their mother daintily hath fed, / Eating the flesh that she herself hath bred. / 'Tis true, 'tis true; witness my knife's sharp point.
Why, there they are, both baked in that pie, which their mother has been daintily eating, feeding on the flesh she gave birth to herself. It's true, it's true: my knife's sharp point bears witness.
Die, frantic wretch, for this accursed deed.
Die, raving wretch, for this cursed deed.
Can the son's eye behold his father bleed?
Can a son's eye see his father bleed?
There's meed for meed, death for a deadly deed.
There's payment for payment, death for a deadly deed.

You sad-faced men, people and sons of Rome, / By uproar severed, as a flight of fowl / Scattered by winds and high tempestuous gusts, / O, let me teach you how to knit again / This scattered corn into one mutual sheaf, / These broken limbs again into one body; / Lest Rome herself be bane unto herself, / And she whom mighty kingdoms curtsy to, / Like a forlorn and desperate castaway, / Do shameful execution on herself. / But if my frosty signs and chaps of age, / Grave witnesses of true experience, / Cannot induce you to attend my words, / Speak, Rome's dear friend, [to Lucius] as erst our ancestor, / When with his solemn tongue he did discourse / To love-sick Dido's sad attending ear / The story of that baleful burning night / When subtle Greeks surprised King Priam's Troy. / Tell us what Sinon hath bewitched our ears, / Or who hath brought the fatal engine in / That gives our Troy, our Rome, the civil wound. / My heart is not compact of flint nor steel, / Nor can I utter all our bitter grief, / But floods of tears will drown my oratory / And break my utterance, even in the time / When it should move you to attend me most, / And force you to commiseration. / Here's Rome's young captain, let him tell the tale, / While I stand by and weep to hear him speak.

You sad-faced men, people and sons of Rome, split apart by uproar like a flock of birds scattered by winds and fierce, stormy gusts: O, let me teach you how to bind this scattered corn together again into one sheaf, and these broken limbs into one body again, in case Rome becomes her own poison, and she to whom mighty kingdoms bow, like a lost and desperate outcast, shamefully destroys herself. But if my white hair and wrinkles of age, solemn witnesses of real experience, cannot persuade you to listen to me, (To Lucius) speak, Rome's dear friend, as our ancestor Aeneas once did when he solemnly told love-sick Dido, who listened sadly, the story of that deadly burning night when the cunning Greeks took King Priam's Troy by surprise. Tell us what Sinon has bewitched our ears, or who has brought in the deadly wooden horse that gives our Troy, our Rome, this wound of civil war. My heart is not made of flint or steel, and I cannot tell all our bitter grief without floods of tears drowning my speech and breaking off my words just when they should most move you to listen and force you to pity. Here is Rome's young captain. Let him tell the story, while I stand by and weep to hear him speak.

Then, noble auditory, be it known to you / That Chiron and the damned Demetrius / Were they that murdered our emperor's brother; / And they it were that ravished our sister. / For their fell faults our brothers were beheaded, / Our father's tears despised, and basely cozened / Of that true hand that fought Rome's quarrel out / And sent her enemies unto the grave. / Lastly, myself unkindly banished, / The gates shut on me, and turned weeping out, / To beg relief among Rome's enemies; / Who drowned their enmity in my true tears, / And oped their arms to embrace me as a friend. / I am the turned-forth, be it known to you, / That have preserved her welfare in my blood / And from her bosom took the enemy's point, / Sheathing the steel in my advent'rous body. / Alas, you know I am no vaunter, I; / My scars can witness, dumb although they are, / That my report is just and full of truth. / But soft, methinks I do digress too much, / Citing my worthless praise. O, pardon me; / For when no friends are by, men praise themselves.

Then, noble listeners, know that Chiron and the damned Demetrius were the ones who murdered our emperor's brother, and they were the ones who raped our sister. For their cruel crimes our brothers were beheaded, our father's tears were scorned, and he was basely tricked out of that loyal hand which fought Rome's wars to the end and sent her enemies to the grave. Lastly, I myself was cruelly banished, the gates shut on me, and sent out weeping to beg for help among Rome's enemies, who drowned their hatred in my true tears and opened their arms to embrace me as a friend. Know that I, the outcast, am the one who has protected Rome's welfare with my blood, taking the enemy's sword point from her breast and sheathing the steel in my own daring body. Alas, you know I am no boaster. My scars, though they are dumb, can bear witness that what I say is just and true. But wait, I think I am straying too far, listing my own worthless praises. O, forgive me: when no friends are near, men praise themselves.

Now is my turn to speak. Behold the child. / Of this was Tamora delivered, / The issue of an irreligious Moor, / Chief architect and plotter of these woes. / The villain is alive in Titus' house, / And as he is to witness, this is true. / Now judge what cause had Titus to revenge / These wrongs unspeakable, past patience, / Or more than any living man could bear. / Now have you heard the truth. What say you, Romans? / Have we done aught amiss? Show us wherein, / And, from the place where you behold us pleading, / The poor remainder of Andronici / Will, hand in hand, all headlong hurl ourselves, / And on the ragged stones beat forth our souls, / And make a mutual closure of our house. / Speak, Romans, speak, and if you say we shall, / Lo, hand in hand, Lucius and I will fall.

Now it is my turn to speak. Look at this child. Tamora gave birth to this, the offspring of a godless Moor, the chief designer and plotter of these sorrows. The villain is alive in Titus's house, and, as wretched as he is, he will confirm that this is true. Now judge what cause Titus had to avenge these unspeakable wrongs, beyond patience, more than any living man could bear. Now you have heard the truth. What do you say, Romans? Have we done anything wrong? Show us where, and from this place where you see us pleading, the poor remains of the Andronici will hurl ourselves headlong, hand in hand, and dash out our souls on the jagged stones, and bring our family to an end together. Speak, Romans, speak, and if you say we must, look, Lucius and I will fall hand in hand.
Come, come, thou reverend man of Rome, / And bring our emperor gently in thy hand, / Lucius our emperor; for well I know / The common voice do cry it shall be so.
Come, come, you respected man of Rome, and lead our emperor gently by the hand, Lucius our emperor. For I know very well that the voice of the people cries that it shall be so.
Lucius, all hail, Rome's royal emperor!
All hail Lucius, Rome's royal emperor!
Go, go into old Titus' sorrowful house, / And hither hale that misbelieving Moor / To be adjudged some direful slaught'ring death, / As punishment for his most wicked life.
Go, go into old Titus's house of sorrow, and drag that unbelieving Moor out here, to be sentenced to some dreadful, killing death as punishment for his most wicked life.
Lucius, all hail, Rome's gracious governor!
All hail Lucius, Rome's gracious ruler!

Thanks, gentle Romans. May I govern so / To heal Rome's harms and wipe away her woe! / But, gentle people, give me aim awhile, / For nature puts me to a heavy task. / Stand all aloof; but, uncle, draw you near / To shed obsequious tears upon this trunk.

Thank you, kind Romans. May I govern so as to heal Rome's injuries and wipe away her sorrow! But, kind people, give me a little time, for nature sets me a heavy task. All stand back. But, uncle, come close and shed mourning tears on this body.
O, take this warm kiss on thy pale cold lips. / These sorrowful drops upon thy blood-stained face, / The last true duties of thy noble son.
O, take this warm kiss on your pale cold lips, and these sorrowful tears on your bloodstained face: the last true duties of your noble son.
Tear for tear and loving kiss for kiss / Thy brother Marcus tenders on thy lips. / O, were the sum of these that I should pay / Countless and infinite, yet would I pay them.
Your brother Marcus offers tear for tear and loving kiss for kiss on your lips. O, even if the number I had to pay were countless and endless, still I would pay them.

Come hither, boy; come, come, and learn of us / To melt in showers. Thy grandsire loved thee well. / Many a time he danced thee on his knee, / Sung thee asleep, his loving breast thy pillow; / Many a story hath he told to thee, / And bid thee bear his pretty tales in mind / And talk of them when he was dead and gone.

Come here, boy. Come, come, and learn from us how to melt into tears. Your grandfather loved you dearly. Many times he bounced you on his knee and sang you to sleep with his loving breast as your pillow. He told you many stories, and asked you to remember his pretty tales and talk about them when he was dead and gone.

How many thousand times hath these poor lips, / When they were living, warmed themselves on thine! / O, now, sweet boy, give them their latest kiss. / Bid him farewell; commit him to the grave. / Do them that kindness, and take leave of them.

How many thousand times these poor lips, when they were alive, warmed themselves on yours! O, now, sweet boy, give them their last kiss. Say goodbye to him and lay him in the grave. Do them that kindness, and take your leave of them.
O grandsire, grandsire, e'en with all my heart / Would I were dead, so you did live again! / O Lord, I cannot speak to him for weeping; / My tears will choke me if I ope my mouth.
O grandfather, grandfather, with all my heart I wish I were dead, if only you could live again! O Lord, I can't speak to him for crying. My tears will choke me if I open my mouth.
You sad Andronici, have done with woes. / Give sentence on the execrable wretch / That hath been breeder of these dire events.
You grieving Andronici, put an end to your sorrows. Pass sentence on the hateful wretch who has been the cause of these dreadful events.

Set him breast-deep in earth and famish him; / There let him stand and rave and cry for food. / If anyone relieves or pities him, / For the offence he dies. This is our doom. / Some stay to see him fastened in the earth.

Bury him chest-deep in the earth and starve him. Let him stand there and rave and cry for food. If anyone helps or pities him, he dies for the offence. This is our sentence. Some of you stay and see him fixed in the earth.

Ah, why should wrath be mute and fury dumb? / I am no baby, I, that with base prayers / I should repent the evils I have done. / Ten thousand worse than ever yet I did / Would I perform, if I might have my will. / If one good deed in all my life I did, / I do repent it from my very soul.

Ah, why should anger be silent and fury dumb? I am no baby, to repent the evil I have done with snivelling prayers. I would do ten thousand worse things than I ever did, if I could have my way. If I ever did one good deed in all my life, I repent it from the bottom of my soul.

Some loving friends convey the emperor hence, / And give him burial in his father's grave. / My father and Lavinia shall forthwith / Be closed in our household's monument. / As for that ravenous tiger, Tamora, / No funeral rite, nor man in mournful weed, / No mournful bell shall ring her burial; / But throw her forth to beasts and birds of prey. / Her life was beastly and devoid of pity; / And being dead, let birds on her take pity.

Let some loving friends carry the emperor away and bury him in his father's grave. My father and Lavinia shall be laid at once in our family's tomb. As for that greedy tiger, Tamora, no funeral rite, no man in mourning clothes, no mournful bell shall ring at her burial, but throw her out to the beasts and birds of prey. Her life was beastly and without pity, and now she is dead, let the birds take pity on her.
